She has one further observation, offered without much comfort. If the cooperative had been given only the sound record, and had been told what the sound record was supposed to mean, it would have concluded in 2019 that the closure had failed. The closure was the thing that worked.

title: The Sweep
text:
Every public library in the state reports one number to the body that funds it, and that number is circulation: how many items left the building on somebody’s card. It is cheap to collect, hard to argue with, and it has shaped what libraries buy for forty years.

In 2014 the Kettleman County system, which runs a main branch and four small ones, began counting something else alongside it. Staff walked the floor four times a day on a fixed schedule and wrote down, on a clipboard, every item they found sitting on a table, a study carrel, or the arm of a chair — anything a person had taken off a shelf and not checked out. They called it the sweep.

The sweep was not invented in Kettleman. The method is ordinary in library work. What was unusual was that Kettleman kept it up for nine years and published what it found.

The two records disagree, and they disagree by collection. For popular fiction, circulation and sweep counts rise and fall together: what people borrow is what people pick up. For local history the two come apart completely. A shelf of county atlases and school yearbooks circulated eleven times in 2019 and appeared in 2,300 sweep entries.

Ceri Adeyemi-Lowe, who directs the system, is careful not to overclaim. The sweep does not show that anybody read anything; it shows that an item was moved. But a collection that is moved two thousand times and borrowed eleven times is doing work of a kind the funding formula cannot see, and in 2016 that shelf had been on a list of candidates for withdrawal on the strength of its circulation alone.

What Adeyemi-Lowe wants understood is not that circulation is a bad measure. It is that circulation measures one particular behaviour — taking a thing home — and that the behaviour is spread unevenly across collections for reasons that have little to do with value. A yearbook is consulted, not read through. A county atlas does not fit in a bicycle basket. Reference material was kept non-circulating by policy for most of a century, and the habit outlived the policy by decades.

The state has not changed its formula. Kettleman still reports circulation, still runs the sweep, and publishes the two side by side with a note explaining what each one counts. Adeyemi-Lowe says the note is the part that matters, and that it took her six years to get it short enough that anyone would read it.

title: The Saxony Violin
text:
The violin came to me in a cardboard box lined with a wool coat, which was how Mr. Vasiliou moved anything he cared about. He had been my teacher for four years by then and had never once let me touch it.

“It is not a gift,” he said. “It is a loan of eighteen months. At the end you will bring it back and tell me what it taught you.” I was sixteen, and I heard only the first half.

The instrument was old and not valuable — a factory violin from somewhere in Saxony, he thought, with a repaired crack under the bass bar that made the low notes go soft in damp weather. Beside the school’s instruments it looked like a brown coat in a rack of black ones.

It was also, for the first six months, unplayable by me. Not because it was difficult. Because it was honest. My school violin had been forgiving in the way a bad microphone is forgiving: it flattened everything, the good and the bad alike, into the same pleasant nothing. The Saxony violin reported. A bow drawn a millimetre crooked came back as a scrape I could not pretend not to hear.

I spent that autumn discovering how much of my playing had been a kind of rounding. I had thought I was in tune. What I had been was close enough for an instrument that could not tell the difference.

I gave it back in the spring of my eighteenth year and told him it had taught me that I was worse than I had thought. He said that was the first half again, and waited. It took me most of another year to reach the second half, which was that for four years he had been hearing everything the school violin was hiding, and had never once said so, because he was waiting for me to have the ears to hear it for myself.

title: Ninety Words on the Wall
text:
The label beside a painting is the most-read piece of writing in any museum and the least-discussed. Visitors give the picture about eleven seconds and the label about twenty. Nobody signs it. In most institutions nobody is told who wrote it, and the writer has ninety words, give or take, in which to decide what a stranger will notice for the rest of their life.

I wrote labels for eleven years. The first thing the job teaches is that a label is not a summary; it is a door held open at a particular angle. Put the date first and the visitor reads a historical document. Put the sitter’s name first and they read a person. Put the pigment first and they read a surface. The painting does not change. The visitor’s eleven seconds change completely, and they change before the visitor knows a choice has been made on their behalf.

This is the objection my colleagues in the curatorial department raised most often, and it is a serious one. A label that steers is a label that forecloses. The purest position holds that the wall should carry the title, the artist, the date, the medium and nothing else — let the work speak. I held that position myself for about two years.

What ended it was a Tuesday in the Dutch gallery. A man in his sixties stood in front of a small winter scene for a long time and then asked me, with real embarrassment, whether it was a photograph. He was not a foolish man. He had simply never been told that anyone had painted in 1608, and the bare label — title, artist, date, medium — had told him nothing he could use. The work had spoken, and he had not been given the language.

So I stopped believing in the silent wall, and I did not start believing in the chatty one. What I came to instead was a rule I could not always keep: a label earns its ninety words only if a visitor who reads it looks back at the painting afterward. A label that sends you to the next room has failed, however elegant it is. A label that makes you look again has done the whole of its job, and it does not matter at all that nobody will ever know who wrote it.

I still test my old labels that way when I visit. Most of them fail. Two or three hold, and I stand in front of those for longer than eleven seconds, which is, I suppose, the only review a label writer ever gets.

title: The Compass in the Eye
text:
A European robin taken from a garden in Germany and released in the dark will still set off toward the southwest. Something in the bird reads the Earth’s magnetic field. What that something is has been argued over for fifty years, and the argument has been unusually productive, because the two candidate answers make predictions that pull apart under test.

The first candidate is mechanical. Tiny crystals of magnetite — the same iron oxide that makes a lodestone — were reported in the upper beak of several migratory species. A crystal small enough will twist toward north like a compass needle, and a nerve ending pressed against it would feel that twist. This is a satisfying idea because it is so concrete: a physical needle, a physical push.

The second candidate is chemical, and much stranger. In the bird’s retina sits a light-sensitive protein called cryptochrome. When a photon strikes it, two electrons can be left briefly unpaired, and the rate at which that pair settles back down depends on the angle of the surrounding magnetic field. The bird would not feel north so much as see it, as a faint pattern laid over whatever else it was looking at.

Two results moved the weight of evidence toward the retina. The first is that robins tested in total darkness lose their bearings, and so do robins under light of the wrong colour — a mechanical needle would not care about either. The second is that a weak oscillating radio-frequency field, far too feeble to move any crystal, scrambles their orientation completely. That is the signature of a chemical reaction sensitive to electron spin, and of almost nothing else.

The mechanical candidate lost further ground when the beak cells that had been taken for magnetite-bearing neurons were examined again. They were macrophages — immune cells that patrol tissue and accumulate iron as part of that work. The cells turned out to be housekeeping, not navigation, and one of the field’s most reproduced images quietly stopped meaning what it had meant.

None of this settles the whole problem, and the honest summary is narrower than the headlines. A compass and a map are not the same instrument. The retinal mechanism explains, robustly, how a bird knows which way is north. It does not explain how a bird displaced a thousand kilometres knows that it has been displaced, or in which direction, and some form of iron-based sensing may yet turn out to be doing that second job. The compass looks solved. The map does not.

title: The First Vote
text:
Twelve people are shown into a room and told to reach agreement. Almost the first decision they make is one nobody instructs them to make: whether to take a vote straight away or to talk first. Researchers who study deliberation call the two habits verdict-driven and evidence-driven, and the difference between them turns out to shape nearly everything that follows.

A verdict-driven room polls early. Hands go up, the split is on the table within minutes, and the conversation that follows is organised around the two camps that now exist. An evidence-driven room does the opposite: it works through what was presented, witness by witness, and postpones any count until the talking has run its course. The first kind of room finishes sooner. The second kind remembers more of the evidence afterward, distributes speaking time more evenly, and is markedly less likely to produce a member who later says they went along with something they did not believe.

The early ballot is not a window opening on the room’s thinking. It is a door closing on it. Once a person has said "guilty" out loud in front of eleven others, the discussion that follows is not an enquiry but a defence, and the strongest predictor of where a jury ends up is simply the size of the majority on that first ballot. Where ten or more agree at the outset, the group nearly always finishes where it started.

This is a striking finding and it comes with a caution that is easy to skip. Real deliberations are closed. Almost everything known about this comes from mock juries — volunteers shown a filmed or transcribed trial and asked to deliberate about a verdict that will not send anyone anywhere. Whether people under no real obligation behave as people under a heavy one do is not a question the studies can answer about themselves.

The caution does not dissolve the finding. Mock juries reproduce the pattern across decades, across countries, and across changes in how the trial material is presented, and a result that survives that much variation is not usually an artefact of the laboratory. But the honest statement is narrower than the headline. What the research establishes is that the order of two ordinary procedural choices changes what a group of people remembers and how evenly they speak. Whether it changes who goes to prison is a claim the evidence gestures at and does not reach.

title: The Unclaimed Shelf
text:
The summer I was seventeen my grandmother put me, her only granddaughter, behind the counter of her shoe-repair shop and told me not to touch anything with a blade on it. The shop smelled of neatsfoot oil and hot rubber, a smell I have never met anywhere else and can still produce in my head at will. Nuala worked at the back on a stitcher older than either of us, and when the machine was running you could not hear a word she said, which suited us both.

Behind the till, running the whole length of the wall, was the unclaimed shelf. Every pair on it had been mended and never collected. Each carried a paper tag in Nuala’s square capitals — a surname, a date, and nothing else — and the dates went back further than I wanted to look. Brown brogues from a decade before I was born. A child’s sandal, one only, with a new strap.

I asked her once why she did not clear it. She said she would clear it when the shop closed and not before, and went back to the stitcher, which I took at the time for the sort of thing old people say instead of answering. I had a theory that summer that she kept the shelf because she could not bear to throw anything out, and I was pleased with the theory, because it explained her without costing me anything.

In August a man came in with a docket so soft it had gone the texture of cloth. He was perhaps fifty and he did not apologise, which I remember because I had expected him to. Nuala read the docket, walked the length of the shelf without counting, and came back with a pair of black boots, resoled, the leather gone the colour of tea. Eleven years, she said, and he said yes. She did not charge him. He did not thank her in any way I would have recognised as thanks; he put a hand flat on the counter for a second and then took the boots and went.

I have thought about the shelf a good deal more than I expected to. It was not that she could not throw things out — she threw out plenty, and had a temper about clutter. It was that a mended thing is a promise somebody made, and she had decided that the promise did not expire on her side just because it had gone quiet on the other. I would like to say I understood that in August. What I understood in August was that I had been wrong in a way that was going to take me years to be right about.

title: The Second Translator
text:
A poem is translated once and then, if it survives, again. The second translator arrives forty or sixty years after the first and finds the field already occupied: there is a version people quote, lines that have entered the language, an idea of what the poet sounds like that was made by somebody else’s ear. Whatever the new translation does, it will be read against that.

The usual defence of retranslating is that the first version has dated. This is true but imprecise, because the part that dates is rarely the part readers notice. The original poem does not age; the receiving language does, and unevenly. A word that was neutral in 1958 has since picked up a smirk. A rhythm that sounded like speech has become the rhythm of an announcement. The translator who worked in 1958 made none of these mistakes. The language simply moved underneath the work while it sat still.

What ages fastest is not vocabulary but the translator’s idea of what a reader will tolerate. Every version encodes a guess about how much strangeness an audience will accept before it puts the book down, and that guess is the most local thing in the whole enterprise. The 1958 version smooths an image into something a reader of 1958 would recognise. The reader of today, who has read sixty years of poetry the first translator had not, does not need the smoothing and can feel it happening.

None of which makes the new version better, and the second translator should be careful about the word. She has advantages the first did not: a dictionary the first worked without, scholarship that settled two disputed lines, and the first translation itself, which she has read and cannot unread. She also has a disadvantage nobody talks about — the poem now reaches her through the first version, and the phrases she is most certain of are sometimes the ones she absorbed rather than chose.

So the honest account is not that the old translation was wrong and the new one is right. It is that a translation is a reading made at a date, and that a poem worth the trouble will support more than one. The versions are not rivals so much as a series, and the series is the only form in which the original is visible at all to someone who cannot read it.

title: Why the Leaves Are Red
text:
Autumn yellow is not a puzzle. The yellow pigments sit in the leaf all summer, hidden under chlorophyll, and when the chlorophyll is dismantled they are simply what is left. Red is another matter. Anthocyanin, the pigment that makes a maple burn, is not uncovered in autumn; it is manufactured in autumn, from scratch, by a leaf the tree is about to drop. A tree spends to make it, and spends late, on a part of itself with days to live. Biologists have offered two explanations, and they are not versions of each other.

The first is protective. Withdrawing nitrogen from a leaf is slow work, and it happens in exactly the weather — cold nights, bright days — that makes the photosynthetic machinery easiest to damage. On this account the red pigment is a sunscreen laid down over the leaf for the fortnight the tree needs to empty it, and the expense buys back more nitrogen than it costs.

The second is a signal. Aphids arriving in autumn must choose a tree to lay eggs on, and a tree that can afford a brilliant display is a tree with defences to spare. The colour, on this account, is an honest advertisement that the insect would do well to read and avoid, honest precisely because a weakened tree could not pay for it. The pigment is doing nothing to the leaf at all; it is talking to something outside the tree.

The two accounts are testable because they predict different maps. If the pigment is a sunscreen, the reddest leaves should be the most exposed ones — the outer canopy, the southern face, the sapling in the open rather than the one under cover. If it is a signal, redness should track the insects instead: strongest in the species aphids specialise on, and answering, over evolutionary time, to how much damage those insects do.

Both maps have come back partly right, which is the least satisfying result available and probably the true one. Exposure does predict redness within a tree; insect pressure does predict it across species. A pigment can do two jobs, and a trait that is cheap to keep once it exists need not be maintained by the pressure that first favoured it. The question "what is the red for" assumes a single answer, and the assumption may be the part that fails.

title: The Understudy
text:
For eleven weeks Nadia had played Beatrice to an empty house. She ran the lines in the corridor behind the scene dock, where the pipes made a sound like distant applause, and she had come to prefer that audience. It never coughed. It never arrived late in the second act with its coat still on.

She knew the part the way you know a road you have walked and never driven. Every turn was hers. When Ivo, who actually played Benedick, missed a cue in the Thursday run, she had felt it a half-second before the silence, the way you feel a step that is not there.

Then Marguerite fell on the stairs outside the rehearsal room — nothing dramatic, a wet flagstone and a bad ankle — and the stage manager found Nadia in the corridor at ten past six and said, without ceremony, that she was on.

What surprised her was not the fear. She had rehearsed the fear too. What surprised her was that the part did not fit the way it had fit alone. Ivo said his first line faster than she had ever heard it, and the line she had built over eleven weeks — the one she had turned over at bus stops — arrived in a room that had already moved past it. She said it anyway. It landed somewhere behind her.

By the middle of the second act she had stopped reciting and started listening. The lines came differently then, not worse, but not hers. Ivo would lean on a word she had never thought to lean on, and her own next line would bend to accommodate it, and she would hear herself say something she had not planned. Twice it was better than what she had planned.

Afterwards, in the corridor with the pipes, the company said the generous things companies say. Marguerite, on a chair with her foot up, said only that Nadia had listened in the second half.

Nadia took it as a compliment, and only later, on the bus, understood it as a diagnosis. She had spent eleven weeks learning a part. She had spent one hour learning a play. The corridor had taught her every word and not one of the things that made the words worth saying, and she thought, with a small cold clarity, that she would have to learn it all again, out loud, in front of people, with the coughing and the coats.

title: The Cost of a Straight Line
text:
Every bus network is an argument about who is worth being late for. The argument is usually conducted in the language of engineering, which makes it easy to miss.

A transit planner given a fixed budget faces one choice before any other: frequency or coverage. Frequency means running buses often on a few corridors, so that a rider can leave the house without consulting a timetable. Coverage means running buses rarely on many routes, so that almost every household is within a short walk of a stop. The same money buys either one. It cannot buy both.

The case for frequency is strong and mostly empirical. Ridership rises steeply once the wait between buses drops below about twelve minutes, because below that threshold the bus stops being an appointment and becomes a utility. Straighten the routes, thin the stops, run the buses every ten minutes, and the same fleet will carry substantially more people. Cities that have redrawn their networks on this principle have seen ridership climb on an unchanged budget.

The case for coverage is harder to put in a chart, which is part of its problem. A route that carries eleven passengers an hour through a low-density suburb is, by the ridership measure, a failure. But some of those eleven have no alternative, and the measure that condemns the route counts a rider who would otherwise drive exactly the same as a rider who would otherwise not go at all. A network optimised purely for ridership will shed precisely the passengers for whom the network is not a convenience but a condition of leaving the house.

Planners know this, and the honest ones say so. One consultant who has run the exercise with dozens of city councils refuses, on principle, to recommend a split. He presents the trade-off, makes the council choose a number — seventy per cent frequency and thirty per cent coverage, or the reverse — and then designs to it. The technical work, he argues, begins only after a political question has been answered politically.

What makes the argument hard is that both sides appeal to fairness and mean different things by it. Frequency treats riders as interchangeable and asks which arrangement moves the most of them. Coverage treats riders as neighbours and asks whether anyone has been left without a bus at all. Neither is a mistake. But a network cannot be drawn to both, and a city that refuses to choose has not avoided the choice. It has only allowed the budget to make the choice for it, quietly, one service cut at a time.

title: The Clock in the Seed
text:
A seed that sprouts in November is a seed that dies in January. Plants of the temperate zone therefore face a problem of measurement: they must be able to tell a warm week in autumn from the spring that follows winter, using information available to something with no eyes, buried under two centimetres of soil.

The solution most temperate species have arrived at is not to measure warmth at all. It is to measure cold, and to require a great deal of it. A dormant seed of many species will not germinate, however favourable the temperature, until it has accumulated a certain number of hours near freezing — a chilling requirement, running in the field from a few hundred hours to a couple of thousand. Warmth alone cannot trigger it. Warmth after enough cold can. The seed is not waiting for spring; it is waiting to have finished winter, which is a different and far more reliable signal.

The mechanism is chemical and, in outline, understood. Abscisic acid holds the seed shut. Prolonged cold degrades it and at the same time builds up gibberellins, which open the seed. The ratio between the two is the clock face. Nothing in it can be run backwards by a mild fortnight, which is precisely the point: a counter that only goes up cannot be fooled by a warm November.

It can, however, be starved. A chilling requirement is a bet that winter will supply a certain quantity of cold, and the bet is placed once, over evolutionary time, against the climate a species grew up in. Winters across much of the temperate zone are now shorter and less cold. Orchardists noticed first, because their trees run on the same system and their livelihoods are annual: in low-chill years, peach and cherry trees leaf out raggedly, flower over three weeks instead of one, and set a fraction of the fruit.

For wild plants the consequence is harder to see and probably larger. A seed that has not met its requirement does not fail loudly. It simply stays shut through a spring that would have suited it, and waits, and spends a little more of a finite reserve, and tries again the following year against a winter likely to be warmer still. The failure looks, from outside, exactly like patience.

title: The Night Bus
text:
For twenty-two years I drove the 11:40 out of Renshaw Street, which is the last bus of the night and the only one that runs the whole loop. For most of those years I was the only woman on the night roster, and I had the 11:40 because nobody else wanted it. By the third stop it is usually empty. You learn to drive an empty bus differently. You stop taking the corners as though someone might be standing, and then one night someone is, and you remember why the rule exists.

There was a man who got on at the fourth stop on Fridays. Mr Ahearn, according to the pass he showed me the first month and never showed again. He sat three rows back on the left, and he rode to the terminus, and he did not get off anywhere in between, which meant he was paying a full fare to end up two miles from where he started with no way home but the walk. I worked out the walk once. Forty minutes, uphill at the end.

I asked him, in the fourth or fifth year, whether there was somewhere he was going. He said he liked the window. I let it alone after that. There is a kind of question you can only ask once, and I had used mine.

The night he did not come I held the bus at the fourth stop with the doors open. The timetable gives you ninety seconds there and I took four minutes, which on that route is nothing, because the whole schedule is built with slack in it for weather and for roadworks and for the drunk who cannot find his pass. Nobody in twenty-two years had ever asked me what I did with mine.

The depot clerk told me on the Monday that he had moved in with his daughter in Carrow. He was not ill. He had simply gone, the way people do, and the Friday bus went on running without him, and I went on holding it at the fourth stop for four minutes for most of another year. I could not have told you what I was waiting for. I can tell you that the slack was there whether I used it or not, and that I had finally found something to spend it on.

title: Why the Queue Moved
text:
The outpatient pharmacy at a large teaching hospital had six counters and, until 2011, six queues. Patients chose one on arrival and stayed in it. The complaint most often recorded in the hospital’s feedback book was not that the wait was long. It was that the wait was unfair: the queue beside yours moved and yours did not, and the person who came in after you left before you did.

In 2011 the pharmacy replaced the six lines with one. Arrivals joined a single winding queue and were called forward to whichever counter came free. Nothing else changed. The same six pharmacists worked the same hours and filled prescriptions at the same rate.

The mean wait did not move. It was fourteen minutes before the change and fourteen minutes after, which is exactly what arithmetic predicts: six servers working at one speed get through the same number of people however the people are arranged in front of them. What changed was the spread. In the year before the change, the slowest one in twenty patients waited forty-one minutes or more. In the year after, that figure was twenty-two.

Recorded complaints about waiting fell by roughly two thirds. The researchers who studied the change argue that this is the whole finding, and that it is a finding about justice rather than about speed. A person in a single queue can see that the order is the order of arrival. A person in one of six queues can see only that somebody else is doing better, and has no way to know whether that is luck or a slower pharmacist or a longer prescription in front of them.

There is a cost, and the paper is careful about it. One queue of forty looks worse from the door than six queues of seven, and a follow-up count found that a small number of patients turned round and left without joining. Those people never appear in a waiting-time statistic, because they never waited. The single queue makes the line honest and, in doing so, makes it harder to look at, and what the counter cannot dispense is the only thing anyone was asking for.

title: The Forger’s Signature
text:
Between 1951 and 1964, Emil Warde painted at least thirty-one Dutch landscapes that had never existed. They were not copies. A copy is a poor business: the original is in a museum, and a second one turning up on the market answers the question before it is asked. What Warde made were new paintings in an old hand, canvases that a seventeenth-century painter might have produced and did not.

That is a far harder thing to do than it sounds, and not for the reasons people assume. The pigments can be sourced and the canvases can be found on the backs of worthless period paintings. The difficulty is that inventing a picture in someone else’s manner requires the forger to make the choices the painter would have made, at the moment the painter would have made them, and to make them without preference.

Warde could not manage the last part. The Amsterdam curator who finally doubted the pictures did not begin with the paint. She began with a feeling, recorded in her notes as an irritation, that the skies were too well organised. A bird in the upper left of one canvas balanced a church tower in the lower right so neatly that the eye had nowhere else to go. She went through the group and found the same tidiness everywhere: compositions closed, horizons placed, nothing left ragged.

The painters Warde was imitating were working men filling orders. They left things in their pictures because the things were there. Warde left nothing in by accident, and that is what gave him away, because a forgery is exposed not by what it fails to imitate but by what it improves.

He served four years. In an interview afterward he said he had never been able to look at one of the real ones without wanting to move something, and he seemed to think this was a confession of taste rather than of crime. In a sense he was right. The eye that let him do it at all was the eye that made every canvas a little too good, and there was no version of him that had one without the other.

title: The Ice That Remembers Air
text:
An ice sheet is a stack of winters. Snow falls, is buried by the next year’s snow, and is slowly crushed into ice, and a core drilled through the stack gives a layered record that can be counted downward like the rings of a tree. Trapped inside that ice are bubbles, and inside the bubbles is air — actual samples of the atmosphere, not a proxy for it. Nothing else on Earth offers that.

The bubbles come with a complication that took some years to appreciate. The top seventy to a hundred metres of an ice sheet are not ice but firn: old snow, compacted but still porous, with its spaces connected to one another and to the surface. Air moves freely through the firn. Only when the pores finally pinch shut, deep down, is a parcel of air sealed off and made into a bubble.

The consequence is that the air in a bubble is younger than the ice around it. It was still circulating, still exchanging with the atmosphere above, during all the centuries the ice enclosing it was being buried. The size of the offset depends on how fast snow piles up. At a coastal site with heavy snowfall the pores close within a few decades and the difference is perhaps thirty years. At a high, cold, dry site in the interior of Antarctica, where a century may add a few centimetres, the same difference can exceed two thousand.

This matters because the questions people ask of an ice core are usually questions about timing. Did carbon dioxide rise before the warming or after it? The temperature signal is read from the ice itself, and the carbon dioxide is read from the air in the bubbles, and the two are on different clocks. Getting an answer means aligning them, and the alignment is not a detail cleaned up at the end. It is most of the work, and its uncertainty is often larger than the interval being argued about.

None of this makes the record less valuable. It makes it a record of two things at once, taken from one column of ice, and a reader who forgets that is reading a calendar with two hands and assuming they agree.

title: The Substitute
text:
My uncle Peter played the organ at St Brendan’s for thirty-one years and was never once the organist. The parish had an organist, a Mr Dolan, who held the post from 1962 until his death, and my uncle was the man they rang when Mr Dolan had shingles, or a wedding in Athlone, or the flu that went round the choir in 1979. He kept his shoes in a canvas bag by the door of the flat, and the bag stayed packed.

I asked him once whether he minded. He was tuning a radio at the time and did not look up. He said that the organist plays what the year requires, the same eleven hymns in the same eleven weeks, and that a substitute plays whatever the morning has left lying about. He said this as though it settled the matter, and for him I think it did.

It was true that he was never given a season. He was given the Sunday after a funeral, the Sunday when half the parish had gone to the match, the eight o’clock in February with nine people in it and the heating off. Those were the mornings when nobody was listening closely, which meant they were the mornings when he could do as he liked, and he did. I heard him take a plain recessional and open it out until it did not want to end, in a church so empty you could hear the pedals.

When Mr Dolan died the parish asked my uncle to take the post. He was sixty-four. He said no, and gave as his reason that he did not want to learn the eleven hymns, which was a joke, and everyone took it as one. He played the funeral, and then went on being rung up, less and less, by a parish that had found somebody younger.

The canvas bag was still by the door when we cleared the flat. I have it now. I have never been able to decide whether the thing he protected all those years was his freedom or only his excuse, and I have stopped believing the two can be told apart from the outside.

title: The Milk at the Back
text:
Everyone who has ever walked into a supermarket for one thing and left with nine knows the explanation, because it is repeated everywhere: the milk is at the back of the shop so that you have to walk past everything else to reach it. The layout is described as a trap, and the shopper as the animal in it.

The story has a flaw that anyone who has worked in a shop will name immediately. Milk arrives on pallets, in volume, several times a week, and it has to go from the lorry into a refrigerated case without spending time in the warmth. The loading bay is at the back. The chillers are at the back because the loading bay is at the back, and the loading bay is at the back because the front of the building faces the car park. The arrangement is older than the marketing literature that claims it.

That does not settle the question of whether the walk sells anything, which is a separate matter and has been studied. The findings are mixed and modest. Shoppers on a short planned trip are extremely resistant: tracking studies find they walk a direct line, look at almost nothing, and buy what they came for. Shoppers without a list behave differently, and the extra aisles do produce extra purchases — but the effect is measured in a few per cent, not in the nine items of the anecdote.

What the research more reliably finds is something less satisfying to repeat. The items that end up in the basket unplanned are overwhelmingly those placed at eye level near the end of an aisle, or beside the tills, or in the path of a queue. Position within reach matters more than distance walked. The trap, if there is one, is not the length of the journey. It is the last four feet of it.

It is worth asking why the back-of-the-shop story survives so well despite being, at best, half true. It flatters everyone. It tells the shopper that the extra items were not a choice, and it tells the retailer that the building is cleverer than it is.

title: What the Sand Knows
text:
A handful of beach sand looks like a single substance, and it is not. It is a crowd of grains from different places, at different ages, that happen to have arrived at the same shore, and there is a mineral in it that can be made to say where each grain came from.

That mineral is zircon. It is common, it is hard, and above all it is stubborn: a zircon grain survives the weathering, transport and burial that destroy almost everything around it, and it can be carried through several cycles of mountain, river, seabed and mountain again without being reset. When a zircon crystallises it takes up uranium and rejects lead almost completely. Any lead found inside it afterward is therefore lead that grew there, by decay, at a known rate — so the grain carries the date of its own crystallisation, locked in and portable.

The method is to pick several hundred zircon grains out of one sand sample and date them individually. What comes back is not a number but a distribution: a spectrum of ages, with peaks. Each peak corresponds to an episode of mountain building somewhere upstream, and the set of peaks is close to a fingerprint, because no two source regions have quite the same history of being built.

The results are regularly startling. Sand on a beach may be dominated by grains eighteen hundred million years old, from rocks that no longer outcrop within two thousand kilometres, delivered by a river system that stopped existing before there were grasses. A beach is not made by its own coastline. It is the end of a queue that may have taken a continent’s lifetime to form.

There are limits, and they are the ordinary ones. Zircon is not produced in equal amounts by every rock, so a source rich in it is over-represented and a basalt province that makes almost none can be invisible however much sediment it contributed. Grains are also recycled, so a peak may record not the rock the sand came from but a much older rock that fed it. The distribution is evidence, not a transcript, and reading it well means knowing what it cannot say.

title: The Sign Painter’s Daughter
text:
My father painted signs for forty years, and for the last ten of them he painted them mostly for people who could not afford to have them painted any other way. The bakery on Carver Street had a vinyl banner by then, cut by a machine in an afternoon, and the pharmacy had a lightbox. What came to him were the jobs nobody had thought to modernise: the name on a fishing boat, the numbers on a church hymn board, a widow who wanted her late husband’s van lettered one last time before she sold it.

I worked with him the summer I was fifteen, which mostly meant cleaning brushes. He had a rule that a brush was not clean until the water ran clear and then ran clear again, and I thought this was the kind of rule old men make up to keep children busy. It took me most of July to understand that the second rinse was for the paint that hides in the heel of the brush, where the bristles meet the metal collar, and that a brush put away with paint in its heel is a brush that will never again make a clean edge.

That was the whole of his trade, as far as I could see: the edge. Anyone could fill in a letter. What he sold was the line where the letter stopped, laid down in one pull of a long-haired brush with his little finger resting on the board to steady it. He called this “the stroke” as though there were only one, and when I asked how long it had taken him to learn it he said he was still learning it, which I took for modesty and have since come to think was simply a description.

I will not pretend the machine was the enemy. It was not. The vinyl letters on the bakery window were perfectly spaced and perfectly straight, and they would outlast anything my father could have painted there, because the sun that fades enamel does very little to vinyl. When the baker asked him, a little embarrassed, what he thought of them, my father looked for a long moment and said they were very good. He meant it. He had no patience for people who pretended that handwork was better at everything, and he said so, more than once, to customers who hired him for sentimental reasons and then complained about the price.

What the machine could not do was the boat. A hull curves in two directions at once, and the name has to be laid out so that it reads straight to someone standing on the quay, which means it cannot actually be straight on the hull. My father would stand on the quay for twenty minutes before he touched a brush, walking a few steps left and a few steps right, and then he would chalk a line that looked wrong from up close and was right from everywhere else. I watched him do this for the Margaret Ann that August, and I remember thinking that it was the first time I had seen anyone solve a problem that did not exist on paper.

He stopped working the winter I turned twenty. His hand had begun to shake a little, not enough that anyone else would notice, but enough that the stroke was no longer one stroke. He did not announce it. He simply started telling people he was booked, and then that he was retired, and the brushes went into a biscuit tin on the top shelf of the garage, clean, every one of them rinsed until the water ran clear twice.

I did not become a sign painter. I have a job in which nearly everything I make is made on a screen and can be undone. But I kept the tin, and every so often I open it and run a thumb across the heel of a brush, and it is still soft. There is nothing in it. He saw to that. I have never been sure whether I keep the tin because of what it holds or because of how carefully it was emptied.

title: The Deep End
text:
My mother learned to swim at fifty-four, in the shallow end of the Harwood Street baths, on Tuesday evenings between the aqua-aerobics class and the lane swimmers who arrived at eight and looked at us as though we were furniture someone had left in the water. She had decided on it in January, in the way she decided most things, which was to announce it at dinner as already arranged. I was to teach her. I had been a lifeguard for two summers at university, and in her view this made me qualified, available and, being her daughter, unable to charge.

She was not a good student, and I was not a good teacher, and for the first three weeks we were mostly two people standing in chest-deep water being polite to each other. She would do anything I asked at the side of the pool. She would kick holding the rail, blow bubbles, float face-down for a count of five with my hand under her stomach. The moment my hand moved away she stood up. It was not panic. It was quicker and quieter than panic, a kind of reflex, and she always looked faintly surprised afterward, as though her legs had made the decision without consulting her.

I tried the things they teach you. I explained that the body floats, that the lungs are two bags of air and she could not sink if she tried. I tried a float board, and then a foam buoy held between the knees, and then simply standing a little further away each week so that the distance was always one she had nearly managed. She listened to all of it with the patience of a woman who has heard a great many explanations in her life and has found most of them to be correct and useless.

What changed it was not anything I did. In the fourth week an old man in the next lane, one of the eight o’clock swimmers, stopped at the wall to catch his breath and watched her stand up for the sixth time. He did not say anything to me. He said to her, “You’re holding your breath like you’re saving it for something.” And my mother laughed, a real laugh, the one she usually kept for other people’s children, and said that she probably was.

It came out on the drive home, in pieces. When she was nine her younger brother had gone under at a lake in Connemara, and she had been the one to see it, and the one to shout, and a man she never saw again had gone in and brought him up coughing. Nobody was hurt. It was a story the family told at Christmas as a funny one, about the man’s ruined shoes. She had never told it as anything else. She said she had not thought about it in years, and then she said that this was not quite true, that she thought about it every time the water came up past her chin.

I would like to say that the telling fixed it, and it did not, not at once. But something had moved. The next Tuesday she let her breath out slowly while she floated, the way the old man had shown her with a hand held flat in front of his mouth, and she stayed down for a count of eight, and then twelve. By Easter she could swim a width. By the summer she could swim a length, badly, with her chin held high like a dog carrying a stick, and she refused every suggestion I made about her stroke on the grounds that it got her to the other end.

I have thought since about how little my explanations had to do with any of it. Everything I told her was true. None of it was what she needed, because she had never doubted that she would float. What she did not believe was that nobody would have to go in after her.

title: Counting Screws
text:
The stocktake at Drummond’s Hardware happened on the last Sunday in March, with the shutters down and the lights on, and it was the only day of the year when the shop was entirely quiet. I was nineteen and had worked there for five months. I had been told the stocktake was dull, and I had looked forward to it anyway, because it seemed to me the one job in the building that could be done perfectly.

I was paired with Mrs Okafor, who had worked at Drummond’s since before the paint counter moved and who was the only person Mr Drummond ever deferred to on anything. We were given aisle six: fixings. Screws, nails, bolts, washers, wall plugs, hooks, hinges, several hundred small cardboard boxes and a wall of plastic drawers, each of them labelled in a hand that had changed three times over the years.

I counted. That was my plan and I held to it. I took down a box of forty-millimetre wood screws, tipped it onto the counter, moved them across in fives with the edge of a ruler, wrote the number on the sheet, and put them back. It took four minutes. There were, I worked out, about three hundred boxes like it in aisle six alone, and I remember feeling not dismay at the figure but a kind of satisfaction, as if the size of the job were proof of its seriousness.

Mrs Okafor did not count. She weighed. She had a small brass scale from the back room, and she would weigh ten screws, and then the box, and divide, and write the answer down, and move on. When a box felt wrong in her hand she weighed it twice. When a drawer looked right she did not open it at all. By eleven o’clock she had done four shelves and I had done one, and she brought me a cup of tea and told me, kindly, that I was going to be there until Wednesday.

I said that her numbers would be wrong. I said it more sharply than I meant to, and she did not seem to mind. She agreed that they would be. Every weighed count, she said, was off by a few, one way or the other, and over a whole aisle the errors cancelled so nearly that nobody had ever been able to find the difference in the accounts. Mine would be exact for every box I finished and missing for every box I did not. “You’d have a perfect count of a third of the shop,” she said. “I’d have a decent count of all of it.”

I kept counting, out of pride, for another hour. Then I took down a box of brass hinges, labelled and priced as brass, that held thirty steel ones instead. Someone had put them back in the wrong box, probably years ago. I would have counted them correctly as thirty and never noticed, because I was looking at the number. When I showed the box to Mrs Okafor she lifted it once, set it down, and said she had marked it as light the year before and had meant to look. Steel is a little lighter than brass, and to her hand the box had simply felt wrong.

She was not smug about it. She said that weighing was useless for anything that was not identical; she would never weigh the drawer of mixed hooks, and she counted those one at a time exactly as I did. The trick, she said, was knowing which kind of thing was in front of you. I have since spent a good part of my working life in jobs that call themselves data, and I have met a great many people who count everything and a great many who count nothing, and very few who could have told you, from the feel of a box, which one it needed.

title: The Box Already Ticked
text:
For most of the twentieth century, saving for retirement through an employer began with a form. A new worker who wanted to join the company pension had to ask for one, fill it in, choose how much of each pay packet to put aside, and hand it back. Many never did. Surveys asked them why, and the answers were reasonable-sounding and various: they could not afford it yet, they meant to get round to it, they did not understand the options. Economists read these answers as preferences. People who did not join, the reasoning went, had weighed the future against the present and chosen the present.

The trouble with that reading appeared when employers began to change a single thing about the form. Instead of asking workers to opt in, some firms enrolled every new employee automatically, at a modest contribution rate, and handed them a form to opt out. The money, the choices and the freedom to leave were all identical. The only difference was which box was ticked before anyone picked up a pen.

The effect was enormous. At firms that made the switch, participation among new hires, which had often hovered around half, rose to something close to nine in ten, and it stayed there. If people had truly preferred the present, the opt-out form should have been busy. It was not. Workers who would never have filled in a form to join did not fill in a form to leave, either.

What made the result hard to explain away was how little else had to change. The firms did not run campaigns or hold seminars on compound interest. They did not raise the employer’s contribution or make the pension more generous. In several cases the switch applied only to workers hired after a particular date, so that two people doing the same job at neighbouring desks, one hired in March and one in May, faced the same choice framed in opposite directions, and ended up, as a rule, with opposite outcomes. It is difficult to argue that the May recruits cared more about their old age than the March ones did.

The finding is now famous, and like most famous findings it is usually told too simply. The version that circulates says that defaults work because people are lazy, and that a clever designer can therefore steer a population wherever it likes by choosing the box. Both halves are shakier than they sound. Inertia is part of it, but so is the quiet message a default sends: a worker who finds herself enrolled at three per cent may reasonably take three per cent to be the amount the employer thinks sensible. Defaults work partly because they are read as advice.

That second mechanism has a cost the enthusiasts rarely mention. In the same studies, many workers who would otherwise have chosen a higher contribution rate stayed at the default instead. The automatic box raised the number of savers and, for some of them, lowered the amount saved. A default that looks like advice is followed by those who needed the advice and by some who did not, and the second group is harder to see, because nothing in their records looks like a mistake.

None of this makes the original finding less important. Millions of people are saving who would not otherwise have been, and the gain is concentrated among younger and lower-paid workers, who were the least likely to fill in the form. But the lesson is not that behaviour can be steered for free. It is that there is no neutral form. Every version of the page has a box ticked or unticked, and whoever designs it is choosing, whether or not they admit to it.

The surveys, in the end, were not wrong about what people said. They were wrong about what it meant. “I meant to get round to it” turned out to be a precise description of a decision nobody had made.

title: The Fine That Kept People Away
text:
The overdue fine is one of the few penalties most people have paid without ever feeling they had done anything wrong. Ten cents a day, then twenty-five, capped at the price of the book; a small sum collected at a desk by someone who seemed faintly embarrassed to ask for it. It seemed the fairest of arrangements. For a century public libraries treated the fine as common sense. A book kept is a book another reader cannot borrow, and a charge that grows by the day gives the borrower a reason to bring it back.

Over the last two decades a growing number of library systems have stopped charging it, and the reasons they give are not sentimental. When librarians looked at who owed fines, they found the debts were not spread evenly. They clustered in a few neighbourhoods, usually the poorest, and among children, whose cards were blocked once the total passed a few dollars. A blocked card does not produce a returned book. It produces a borrower who stops coming.

Librarians had long suspected this from the desk. A child would come in with a parent, discover that the card was blocked, and leave without the book she had chosen, and the parent, not wanting to go through it again, would not bring her back. The fine had been set at a level meant to be trivial, and for most borrowers it was. For the ones it was not, it was a closed door.

The fear, when fines were abolished, was that books would stop coming back. In the systems that have published their figures, this mostly did not happen. Return rates held roughly steady, and in several places the number of items returned went up, because borrowers who had been staying away with a book at the bottom of a bag, ashamed of the sum that had built up on it, came back once the sum was forgiven. One city reported that in the month after it cleared old debts, books overdue for years began arriving in the returns chute with notes of apology tucked inside.

Fines, it turned out, had been doing a different job from the one they were designed for. They had not been prompting punctual returns so much as sorting borrowers: those who could pay kept borrowing, and those who could not quietly left. The money collected was small, often less than the staff time spent collecting it. In one system that studied its own records, the borrowers most likely to owe more than a few dollars were also the ones least likely to have visited at all in the previous year. What the fine mainly produced was absence.

It would be too neat to stop there, and the libraries themselves do not. Most still charge for books that are lost outright, because a lost book has to be replaced and someone has to pay for it. Some saw a rise in the number of items kept a few days late, which matters little for a novel nobody else wants and more for a popular new title with a waiting list of forty. And a few administrators have admitted that the policy is hard to evaluate cleanly, because it was usually introduced alongside other changes, such as longer opening hours, automatic renewals and reminder emails, that may deserve some of the credit.

Still, the direction of the evidence is hard to miss, and it points somewhere uncomfortable for anyone who designs penalties. A fine is supposed to change behaviour by attaching a cost to it. But a cost that one person barely notices can be, for another, the reason they stop showing up at all, and a penalty that drives away the very people an institution exists to serve has failed even if every book on the shelf is accounted for.

The libraries did not become more lenient. They became more accurate about what the fine had been for.

title: Two Views on Closing the High Street to Cars
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by an urban planner. Passage B is adapted from an essay by an economist. Both concern closing a town’s main shopping street to motor traffic.
text:
PASSAGE A

When a town proposes closing its main street to cars, the first people to object are almost always the shopkeepers, and their objection is almost always the same: our customers drive. It is a reasonable fear and, in most of the towns that have tried it, a mistaken one. Shopkeepers consistently overestimate how many of their customers arrive by car, sometimes by a factor of two, for a simple reason. The customer who drives is the one who complains about parking, and complaints are what a shopkeeper hears. Surveys that stop people on the pavement and ask how they arrived tell a different story from the one heard at the till.

What happens after a closure is more interesting than the argument before it. Footfall usually rises, though not at once; there is often a dip of a few months while habits adjust. People on foot visit more often and spend less each time, which adds up to more over a month. They also linger. Cafés put tables out. Noise falls, and so, measurably, does the pollution that collects in a narrow street lined with buildings. Rents on the street, in several towns, rose within two years, which is not what landlords do when they believe trade has collapsed. A street that was a route becomes a place, and a place is somewhere people go without needing an errand.

I will concede the obvious: not every business wins. A shop that sells heavy goods, such as paint, furniture or bags of compost, can lose customers who genuinely need to load a car at the door, and a closure planned without loading bays or short-stay parking nearby is a closure planned badly. But the answer is to plan it well, not to leave the street to traffic. The question a town should ask is not whether anyone will lose, but whether the street as a whole will be more used, and on that question the evidence is fairly consistent. Towns that have closed a street and then reopened it to cars are rare, and that rarity is itself a kind of evidence.

PASSAGE B

The studies that show pedestrian streets thriving have a quiet selection problem. Towns do not close streets at random, any more than a gardener plants in the worst soil in the garden. They close the ones that already have heavy foot traffic, attractive buildings and a council with money to spend on paving and benches, and then they measure what happens. A rise in visitors after the change may owe as much to the new paving, the new benches and the publicity as to the absence of cars. A comparison of before and after is only as good as the before, and here the before was chosen precisely because it looked promising.

There is also the matter of where the customers came from. A shopping street is not a closed system. If footfall rises on the pedestrianised street, some of it has usually been drawn from the streets around it, and the shops on those streets rarely feature in the evaluation. Traffic, too, goes somewhere: the cars that used the high street now use the road behind it, and the people who live on that road were seldom asked. A council that counts only the people on the new plaza is counting the winners.

None of this means closures fail. Some plainly succeed, and I would not want to drive through a good many of them again. It means that the evidence usually offered is weaker than its confidence suggests, and that the towns most in need of a lift, the ones with half-empty streets and little money, are exactly the ones the celebrated examples tell us least about. A struggling street with the cars taken away may simply be a quieter struggling street. What would persuade me is a closure in an ordinary town, on an ordinary budget, measured against a similar town that left its street alone.

title: Notes in a Cook’s Hand
text:
My grandmother’s recipe box holds a hundred and twelve index cards, and almost none of them is a recipe in the sense a cookbook would recognise. The card for soda bread lists four ingredients and no quantities. The card for a lemon cake gives the oven temperature in a unit no oven has used for fifty years. A card headed only “Sunday” contains a single instruction, “start the night before,” and nothing else at all. Several are stained so thoroughly with butter that the writing shows through from the back. None is dated, and none is signed, because there was never any question whose they were.

It would be easy to treat such cards as failed documents, recipes that were never properly written down. I think that gets them backward. They were not written for a stranger. They were written by a cook for herself, or for someone who had stood beside her at the stove, and they record only the part that could not be carried in the hands. Everything the body already knew was left out, because writing it down would have been like writing down how to hold a spoon.

Read that way, the cards become a different kind of text, and a surprisingly exact one. Their silences are information. A card that gives the sugar to the quarter ounce and the flour as “enough” tells you which of the two she had once got wrong. The crossings-out tell you more. On the card for gingerbread, the amount of treacle has been changed three times, each time in a different ink, and in the margin, in pencil, is the word “Harrison’s,” which I eventually worked out was the name of a grocer who closed in 1974. After that, presumably, the treacle was never quite right again, and the card records the search for it.

Cookbook writers have always known that a recipe is a compressed thing, and the best of them try to put back what compression leaves out: how the batter should look, what the pan should sound like, when to stop trusting the timer. That is a real achievement, and I do not want to belittle it. A good printed recipe lets someone who has never met you cook your food. But it is a different achievement from the card’s, and not simply a better one. The printed recipe addresses everyone and so must assume nothing. The card addresses almost no one and can assume almost everything. A cookbook that assumed as much as the cards do would be useless to its readers; a card that explained as much as a cookbook does would have been faintly insulting to the person it was written for.

There is a loss in that, and it is the obvious one. Much of what my grandmother knew went with her, because it was never on the cards to begin with. I have made the soda bread perhaps thirty times from her four words, and it is good, and it is not hers. I have tried adding what the printed recipes say, the buttermilk measured, the oven set, the loaf tapped underneath for a hollow sound, and it has made the bread more reliable without making it any more hers. What I have is not her knowledge but its outline, the shape of the gaps where her knowledge used to be.

Yet the outline is not nothing. Historians who study ordinary writing, such as letters, account books and the notes people leave for themselves, have learned to read omission as carefully as statement, because what a writer does not bother to say is a map of what she could take for granted. A recipe card is a small, stubborn instance of this. It tells you, with some precision, what one woman in one kitchen already knew, and so it tells you something no cookbook can: what it was like to be the person for whom all of this was obvious.

title: What a Rest Is For
text:
Every student of music learns the rest before she learns to respect it. A rest is written on the page like a note: it has a shape, a place on the staff, a length measured in beats. And so for a long time it is treated as a note that happens to be silent, a gap to be counted and got through before the next real thing. The student plays the notes beautifully and then sits through the rests as if in a waiting room. Most teachers can recall the moment a particular student stopped counting rests and started playing them, and most can describe what changed only in the vaguest terms.

I want to try to be less vague. A rest is not an absence of sound. In a concert hall it is almost never silent: the last note is still dying away in the room, a string is still faintly ringing, the audience is breathing. What the rest removes is not sound but the performer’s next action, and what it leaves behind is attention with nowhere to go. That is why a rest can be the loudest moment in a piece. Everyone in the hall is waiting, and waiting is a kind of listening with the volume turned up.

Composers have always known this, and some have been ruthless about it. There are passages in the orchestral repertoire where the whole orchestra stops dead for a full bar, and the effect is not of a pause but of a floor giving way. A player who treats that bar as a chance to breathe has not made a mistake that anyone could name, but has made the passage smaller. The rest was the event, and it was spent. Some composers mark such a silence with a pause sign, which tells the performer to hold it for as long as seems right, and so hands the most important decision in the passage to the person in the room.

The difficulty is that a rest cannot be practised the way a phrase can. You can play a difficult run a hundred times until your fingers know it. You cannot rehearse a silence into shape in the same way, because its shape depends almost entirely on what came before it and on the particular room: how long the hall holds a sound, how still the audience is that night, whether someone has just coughed. A rest that was perfectly judged on Tuesday may be a beat too long on Wednesday, and no metronome will tell you. Recordings hide this, since a silence on a recording is always the same length and always in the same room.

This is where I part company with a certain kind of advice, the kind that says silence is the most important part of music. It is a lovely thing to say and it is not quite true. A rest has no meaning of its own; it borrows all of it from the notes on either side. A bar of silence after a single held note means nothing in particular. The same bar after a phrase that has been building for a minute can stop a room. The rest is powerful exactly as the music around it is powerful, and a performer who plays the notes carelessly will find that the silences have nothing to hold. Silence is not the most important part of the music; it is the part that shows most plainly whether the rest of it was earned.

What the good rest asks of a performer, then, is a kind of trust. Having played something well, you must stop and let it go on working without you, and resist the urge to fill the space in case what you played was not enough. Young players rush rests because silence feels like exposure; for a few seconds there is nothing to hide behind, and every listener knows it. Older ones learn, if they are lucky, that the silence is where the listener finally catches up.

title: Two Views on the Glass Case
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by a museum educator. Passage B is adapted from an essay by a museum curator. Both concern whether visitors should be allowed to handle objects.
text:
PASSAGE A

For most of their history museums were places where you were not allowed to touch anything, and for most of that history the rule was plainly right. Objects are fragile, hands are oily, and a single careless visitor can do in a moment what a century of display did not. I have no quarrel with the glass case for the objects that need it. My quarrel is with the assumption, built into nearly every gallery, that looking is the only way of knowing a thing.

A Bronze Age axe head behind glass is a shape and a label. The same axe head in the hand, or, more realistically, a careful replica of it, is a weight. You feel at once that it was made to be swung, that its balance sits toward the blade, that a person who used it all day would have had forearms you do not. Children who handle such objects ask better questions afterward, and so, in my experience, do adults, who tend to forget that they learned the world with their hands long before they learned it with their eyes. A museum that offers only the eye is teaching one sense to do the work of five.

The objection I hear most is that a replica is not the real thing. That is true, and the label should say so plainly. But the real thing in a case is not fully present either; it is present to one sense and absent to all the rest. A visitor who has held the replica returns to the case and sees the original differently, as something heavy, worn and used. Asked afterward what they remembered, visitors who had handled the replica tended to describe the original as well. A handling table does not replace the gallery. It gives visitors a second way in, and very often it is the way that sends them back to the first.

PASSAGE B

Every few years someone discovers that museums are too quiet and too distant, and proposes that visitors be allowed closer. The proposals are generous in spirit, and some of them are good. But they usually rest on a view of the glass case as a barrier, something standing between the visitor and the object, a regrettable necessity to be kept only where damage would otherwise follow, and I think that view misunderstands what a case does.

A case does not only protect. It frames. By removing an object from the reach of the hand, it removes it from the world of use and places it in the world of attention. A spoon on a kitchen table is a spoon; a spoon alone in a lit case asks to be looked at as something made, by someone, at a particular time. That shift is not a loss of meaning. It is where much of a museum’s meaning comes from, and it is available almost nowhere else. Anyone who has watched visitors at a handling table knows how quickly an object in the hand becomes an object to be put down; an object behind glass cannot be put down, and so, sometimes, it is looked at for longer.

I do not object to handling tables; I have set up several myself, and children love them. My concern is with the claim that touching a replica is a deeper kind of knowing than looking at an original. A handling table is good at teaching what things of a kind were like; a case is good at showing what one particular thing was. A replica can teach you the weight of an axe. It cannot teach you that this axe, and no other, was dropped into a river four thousand years ago, and that the scratch along its blade was made before anyone we could name was born. That knowledge is carried by the object alone, and the glass is what keeps it there.

title: The Pull at the Top of the Tree
text:
A tall tree moves hundreds of litres of water a day from its roots to its leaves, some of it more than a hundred metres straight up, and it does so without a pump. There is no heart in a tree and no muscle anywhere in its trunk. The question of how the water gets to the top occupied botanists for most of the nineteenth century, and the answer they eventually settled on still strikes many people, when they first hear it, as too strange to be true.

The obvious candidates fail. Water can be pushed up from below by pressure in the roots, and in some plants in spring it is; cut a grapevine early in the season and it will weep sap. But root pressure can lift water only a few metres, and in many trees it is absent altogether during the summer, when the demand for water is greatest. Capillary action, the tendency of water to creep up a narrow tube, is real too, but in tubes as wide as a tree’s it accounts for a metre or less. Neither comes close.

The answer is that the water is not pushed. It is pulled, from the top. Each leaf is dotted with tiny pores, and through them water evaporates into the air. As a molecule leaves the wet surface inside a leaf, it tugs on the molecules behind it, because water molecules cling to one another with surprising strength. Those molecules tug on the ones behind them, and so on down an unbroken column that runs through the wood of the trunk and into the roots. The sun, by driving evaporation, does the work. The tree simply provides the plumbing. This is why a tree draws up the most water on sunny, breezy days and the least on still, humid nights: the pull tracks the drying power of the air, not anything the tree decides.

The strange part is the state the water is in. A column being pulled from above is under tension, like a rope rather than a pile of bricks, and water under tension is in a condition that ordinary experience does not prepare us for. The conduits themselves are dead cells, hollow tubes with their contents gone, which is part of why the tree spends no energy on the lift. Pull on water in a wide pipe and it breaks: a bubble forms and the column snaps. In the narrow conduits of the wood, water can withstand tensions far beyond anything a suction pump could achieve. A pump at the top of a tall building cannot draw water up more than about ten metres; a tree does many times better every sunny afternoon.

It does not always get away with it. On hot, dry days the tension can become so great that the column does break, and a bubble of air forms inside a conduit, blocking it. Botanists listening to trees with sensitive instruments have heard these failures as faint clicks. A tree survives them because it has built in a great deal of redundancy, with thousands of parallel conduits and small pits between them that let water detour around a blockage, and because some species can refill emptied conduits at night. The system is not so much safe as forgiving.

Physicists who first heard the explanation were sceptical, and some remained so for decades, because it required water to behave in a way that laboratory experiments had rarely shown. It took careful measurements in living trees, with instruments clamped to branches and leaves, before the doubt faded. The instruments showed the tension rising through the morning as the sun climbed and easing again at dusk, as the theory said it should. Even now there are details, especially about how refilling works, that are argued over. But the central idea has held: every tall tree is a column of water hanging from its leaves, held together by nothing more than the attraction of one molecule for the next.

title: The Window That Did Not Flow
text:
Visitors to old churches are often told a small, satisfying fact about the windows. Look closely at a pane of very old glass, the guide says, and you will see that it is thicker at the bottom than at the top. The reason, the guide goes on, is that glass is not really a solid at all but an extremely slow liquid, and over the centuries it has sagged under its own weight, like honey sliding down the inside of a jar. It is the kind of fact that gets repeated at dinner tables and in science classrooms alike.

The observation is often correct. Many old panes really are uneven, and it is true that glass is an odd material. It has no crystal structure; its atoms are frozen in the same disordered arrangement they had as a liquid, and physicists argue, with some heat, about exactly what to call such a state. Even the comparison with a liquid has a respectable history, since scientists of an earlier age did loosely describe glass that way. The fact is appealing because it takes something true and strange and turns it into something you can see.

The explanation, though, does not survive a look at the numbers. The viscosity of ordinary window glass at room temperature has been estimated, and although the estimates vary enormously, even the most generous of them imply that a pane would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag by a visible amount. Old glass, which contains more impurities than modern glass, flows somewhat more readily, but not by nearly enough to close the gap. If glass flowed at the rate the guide’s story requires, the lenses in century-old telescopes would have lost their shape. They have not. Museums hold Roman glass vessels nearly two thousand years old whose walls show no sign of having slumped.

The thickness comes from how the glass was made. Before modern methods, window glass was often produced by spinning a blob of molten glass into a wide, flat disc. The disc was never even, and panes cut from it varied in thickness from one side to the other. A later method, which blew a long cylinder of glass, slit it and flattened it, gave more even panes, but still not uniform ones. Glaziers fitting such panes had a choice about which way up to put them, and it seems that most, sensibly, put the heavier edge at the bottom. But not all. Surveys of old windows have found panes installed with the thick edge at the top, and at the sides, which is exactly what one would expect if the unevenness came from manufacture, and exactly what the flowing-glass story cannot explain.

The story persists anyway, and it is worth asking why. Partly it is that the correct explanation is duller: a manufacturing quirk and a glazier’s habit, rather than a solid that is secretly a liquid. It also flatters the listener, who is let in on a secret: the window looks still, but you, now, know better. Partly it is that the story is not entirely false. Glass really is structurally like a liquid, and in principle it does flow, only so slowly that no one could ever see it happen. The myth takes a real fact about the material and attaches it to the wrong evidence.

That is a common shape for a durable error. A pure invention is easy to dislodge, because nothing props it up. An error that leans on something true is much harder, because every time someone checks the true part, it holds, and the error borrows its credibility. The cure is not to deny the true part but to show exactly where it stops. The window, in the end, tells us a great deal about how glass was made and hung, and almost nothing about how it behaves over time. The sag is in the story, not in the pane.

title: The Odometer in a Bee
text:
A honeybee that has found a good patch of flowers comes home and tells her sisters where it is. She does this by dancing: on the vertical face of the comb she runs a short straight line, waggling her body as she goes, then circles back and runs it again. The angle of the run gives the direction of the food relative to the sun. The length of the waggle gives the distance. A recruit who watches the dance can fly straight to a patch she has never seen.
