Decoding the dance was one of the triumphs of twentieth-century biology, and it left behind a question that took another half-century to answer. The bee reports a distance. How does she know it?

The first guess was energy. Flying is hard work, and a bee that had flown further would have burned more fuel; perhaps she measured the trip by how tired she was. Experiments cast doubt on this. Bees made to carry small weights did not report longer distances, and bees trained to a feeder raised high above the ground reported shorter ones, although the climb had cost them more. Whatever the bee was measuring, it was not simply effort. The idea had been sensible, and some early observations, in which bees flying into a headwind seemed to report longer trips, had appeared to support it.

The answer came from a set of experiments with tunnels. Researchers trained bees to fly down a narrow tunnel to reach a feeder, and lined the walls with patterns. When the walls were covered in fine vertical stripes, a bee that had flown only a few metres came home and danced as if she had flown hundreds. When the stripes were turned to run lengthwise, along the direction of flight, the same short trip produced almost no waggle at all. The bees were not measuring distance directly. They were measuring how much the world had streamed past their eyes. The dance, in other words, was reporting scenery.

This quantity is called optic flow, and it is exactly what you experience looking out of a train window: nearby fence posts race past, while distant hills barely move. A bee flying close to a patterned wall sees an enormous amount of flow; a bee flying high across an open field sees much less for the same distance. For a bee flying at a steady height over the same kind of ground, more flow means more ground covered, and the bee seems to keep a running total of it over the whole trip. The tunnel had simply exaggerated the flow, and the bee’s odometer had read it faithfully.

At first this looks like a flaw. An odometer that can be fooled by wallpaper seems a poor instrument. But consider what the dance is for. A distance in metres would be of little use to a recruit with no way of measuring metres. The bee is not reporting distance to a surveyor; she is reporting it to other bees, who will fly the same route, past the same hedges and over the same fields, and see the same flow. An error built into the route is an error shared by everyone who follows it, and a shared error cancels. The measurement is wrong in a way that does not matter.

The odometer does have limits. Over open water, where the surface below offers little to see, dancers have been found to report distances shorter than the real ones, and a recruit who follows the dance but takes a different path from the dancer may land short or long. The system works because bees from one hive tend to fly the same corridors, day after day. It is not a map of the world. It is a record of what the world looked like on the way, and it is useful precisely because the next bee will see the same thing.

title: The Rain Gauge
text:
I was sent to my great-aunt Ruth’s for the month of June because my parents had decided, on evidence I considered thin, that I needed “a change of air.” Ruth lived alone at the end of a gravel road with a vegetable garden, two cats who did not acknowledge me, and no internet connection worth the name. I had brought a phone I intended to use constantly, and by the second evening I had learned that it found a signal only when I stood on the lid of the rain barrel, which Ruth watched me do without comment.

What I had not been told about was the gauge. It stood in the middle of the back lawn on a wooden post: a brass funnel about the width of a dinner plate that emptied into a narrow tube inside a larger cylinder. Every morning at seven, whether or not it had rained, Ruth walked out in her dressing gown, lifted the funnel, drew out the tube, and read the water level against the marks on a wooden measuring stick. Then she came inside and wrote the figure, to the hundredth of an inch, on a printed card that she mailed to the weather service at the end of each month.

I asked her, on about the fourth morning, why anyone still bothered. There was radar. You could look up how much rain had fallen on any square mile of the country without getting your slippers wet. Ruth considered this while she poured the water out onto the grass. Radar, she said, was very good at telling you where rain was going, and she would not trade it for anything if she were planning a picnic. But radar did not measure rain. It measured something bouncing back from the sky and made a sophisticated guess about what would reach the ground. The gauge was not a guess. It was the rain itself, caught and counted.

She had been doing this for forty-one years. The cards went back in shoeboxes to a spring when she was younger than my mother, and there was a gap in them exactly once: a single morning in March, eleven years earlier, when she had been in the hospital. On the card for that day she had written, in the space for the figure, “no reading.” I pointed out that she could easily have estimated it from a neighbour’s gauge. She looked at me as though I had suggested forging a signature. An honest gap, she said, told the people using the record exactly what they did not know. A guess told them something false and let them believe it.

I did not understand who these people were until a man from the university drove out in the second week to check that the post was still level. He was a hydrologist, and he was more excited about Ruth’s shoeboxes than anyone I had ever seen be excited about anything made of cardboard. A single year of rainfall, he told me, tells you almost nothing, because single years are wild. It is only when you have forty of them, taken the same way in the same place by the same careful person, that the slow changes begin to show through the noise, the way a face shows through a crowd if you look long enough. Ruth, standing behind him, said nothing, but she did not look displeased.

On the twenty-third of June she turned her ankle on the back step, badly enough that she could not walk. At a quarter to seven the next morning she was sitting up in bed, waiting, and it took me a moment to understand what she was waiting for. I went out in my socks. The tube held water to a level just below one of the marks, not quite on it, and I stood there longer than I needed to, aware that nobody on earth would ever know if I simply wrote down the mark. Then I counted the small lines again, got the same awkward number, and wrote that.

Ruth read the card when I brought it in, nodded once, and handed it back for me to put in the box. It is not much of a story. I have told it, over the years, to people who expected it to end with me falling in love with weather, and it does not; I became an accountant. But I have never since been able to round a number I was unsure of without seeing that brass funnel, and the small, stubborn line just under the mark, and a woman in a dressing gown who would rather leave a hole in forty-one years than fill it with something she had not seen.

title: The Word I Knew
text:
The regional spelling bee was held in the gymnasium of a high school I had never seen before, and I remember the smell of floor polish better than I remember the faces of any of the other thirty-eight children. We sat on folding chairs on a low stage built of plywood, facing an audience of parents who had been asked not to make any sound at all. I was eleven. I had been told that I was a good speller so often and by so many adults that I had come to regard it the way I regarded my brown eyes: not an accomplishment, exactly, but a fact about me that other people seemed to find important.

Most of the credit, or the blame, belonged to my father. For two winters he had sat across the kitchen table from me after dinner with a shoebox of index cards, reading out words in the careful, slightly formal voice he used on the telephone. He could not spell them himself. He had left school at fifteen to work in a print shop, and he told me once that in thirty years of setting type by hand he had learned to copy any word perfectly and to spell almost none of them. So he held each card close to his face, checked every letter I said against it with his finger, and said “good” in a way that meant more than the word.

The rules of the bee were simple and merciless. The pronouncer read out your word; you could ask for its definition, its language of origin, or to hear it in a sentence; and then you spelled it aloud, one letter at a time, with no chance to take a letter back. A small bell rang when you were wrong. It was not a loud bell. It did not need to be.

I lasted six rounds. In the seventh I was given “mnemonic,” a word my father and I had practised so many times that the card had gone soft at the corners. I knew it. I want to be clear about that, because the story is not that I did not know it. I asked for the language of origin, which I did not need, because I wanted a few more seconds in which to feel sure. Then I opened my mouth and said “n,” and heard it, and could not take it back. The silent letter I had been drilled on for two winters had simply not come out first. The bell rang, and I walked off the stage and down the steps and sat beside my father in the third row, and neither of us said anything until we were in the car.

I had spent the walk to the parking lot preparing for his disappointment. I had my defence ready: I knew it, it was a slip, it could have happened to anyone. I did not get to use it. He started the engine, sat for a moment with his hands on the wheel, and then began to laugh, quietly at first and then with his shoulders shaking. When he could speak, he told me he had been hoping for about a year that I would lose early one of these times so that we could stop. He had thought I loved the cards. He had kept them going for me.

I had kept them going for him. I had thought, with the complete certainty of an eleven-year-old, that the cards were the one thing he and I did together that made him proud in a way he could say out loud, and I had been afraid that if I stopped winning he would have nothing left to say “good” about. We sat in the parking lot for a long time working this out, two people who had each been generously enduring something for the other’s sake and had never once thought to ask.

I do not want to make it sound as if the bee was a waste. I can still spell almost anything, which has been useful in small ways for forty years, and I have a better eye for a misplaced letter than most of the editors I have worked for. But when people ask me about that afternoon, expecting a story about nerves or about the unfairness of a silent letter, I find I cannot tell it that way. I knew the word. I had known it for two winters. The word was never the thing I did not know.

title: The Road Test
text:
The letter from the licensing office arrived in October, and my father read it at the kitchen table twice before handing it to me as though it were addressed to someone else. At eighty-four, it said, he would need to pass a road test to renew his licence. It was a form letter. Every driver his age in the state received one. He took it personally anyway, which I should have expected from a man who had once written to a newspaper to complain that its crossword was getting easier. He had driven for sixty-three years without, by his own account, a single mistake worth mentioning.

I should say plainly, because it does me no credit, that I hoped he would fail. Not dramatically. I did not want him to run a red light or clip a cyclist. I wanted a calm stranger with a clipboard to tell him, in an official voice, the thing that my brother and I had been failing to say for two years: that his reactions had slowed, that he drifted toward the centre line on bends, that the dent in the rear bumper had not, as he claimed, been put there by someone in the supermarket car park. I wanted the state to do my job for me.

He prepared as though for an examination in a subject he had once taught. He reread the driver’s handbook, which had changed a good deal since 1961, and he was indignant about several of the changes, particularly the one concerning roundabouts, which he regarded as a foreign idea that had been let in without proper scrutiny. He practised parallel parking on the quiet street behind the library, with me in the passenger seat and two orange traffic cones I had bought for the purpose. He was not good at it. He was, I noticed, getting better, and I found I had mixed feelings about that.

The examiner was a woman of about thirty with a ponytail and an expression of total neutrality, which I suppose is a professional requirement. My father shook her hand with the formality he used on bank managers and got behind the wheel. I watched them pull out of the lot and then sat on a bench beside a vending machine for twenty-two minutes, which I know because I checked my watch perhaps forty times. I rehearsed what I would say when he failed. I would be kind. I would not say that I had seen it coming. I would offer to drive him to the library on Tuesdays.

He passed. The examiner told me so herself, walking back across the lot a few steps ahead of him: a couple of points off for a wide turn, she said, but nothing she could fail him for. The new licence, she explained, would be posted to him within the week. She seemed to think I would be pleased. My father came up behind her holding the printed result in both hands like a diploma, and I said congratulations in a voice that I hoped sounded more like congratulations than it felt.

What happened next I have thought about many times since. He did not get back into the driver’s seat. He walked around the car, opened the passenger door, and held the keys out to me across the roof. I asked him what he was doing. He said that he had wanted to know whether he could still pass, and now he knew, and that was enough. He did not want to drive anymore; he had not wanted to for some time. What he had wanted even less was to be told he couldn’t, by me or my brother or anyone else, before he had found out for himself.

I drove us home. He sat beside me with the certificate on his knee, commenting on my following distance, which he considered inadequate, and on my use of the indicator, which he considered theatrical. I have sometimes wished that I had understood him sooner, and sometimes been glad that I didn’t, because if I had, I might have tried to give him the decision myself, gently, over a cup of tea, and it would not have been the same thing at all. A decision that someone hands you is a kindness. He had wanted the other kind, the kind you take.

title: Thirty Percent of What?
text:
Tomorrow, the forecast says, there is a thirty percent chance of rain. Most people who hear this feel that they have been told something, and most of them could not say what. Ask a roomful of them and you will get answers that sound equally confident and are not compatible with one another. It will rain for thirty percent of the day. It will rain over thirty percent of the region. Thirty percent of forecasters think it will rain. None of these is what the forecaster meant.

What the forecaster meant is narrower and, once explained, not difficult. On days when the weather looks like tomorrow’s, measurable rain falls at the forecast location on about three days in ten. The number is a statement about a class of days, not about hours or square miles. It says nothing about how hard the rain will be or how long it will last. A thirty percent chance of a brief shower and a thirty percent chance of a downpour are, as numbers, the same number. The figure also speaks only of the place named; a town ten miles away has a forecast of its own.

When psychologists put the question to ordinary people in several cities in Europe and the United States, they found that the confusion was not random. In some cities most people chose the correct reading; in others, most chose “thirty percent of the time” or “thirty percent of the area.” The pattern tracked how long each city’s forecasters had been broadcasting probabilities and how they had explained them, if at all. Where forecasters had simply announced a number for years and trusted listeners to work it out, listeners had worked out several different things. People were not failing at arithmetic. They were answering a question that nobody had told them how to ask.

That finding cuts against a common complaint, which is that the public simply cannot handle probability and should be spared it. The complaint has something to it. Numbers invite a false precision, and a listener who hears “thirty percent” may treat it as more exact than any forecaster believes it to be. It is also true that words have their own advantages: “a chance of showers” is easier to remember on the way out the door. But words are not a cure. Studies that ask people to put a number on “likely” or “possible” get answers spread so widely that two listeners hearing the same word may be acting on estimates that differ by half. Words do not remove the uncertainty. They hide the disagreement about it.

There is a quieter problem on the forecaster’s side. Rain that arrives unforecast is remembered; sunshine that arrives despite a warning is forgotten, or remembered fondly. A forecaster who is blamed only for the first kind of error has a reason to lean toward warning, and some commercial services have been reported to nudge low probabilities upward for exactly this reason. A day the model gives a five percent chance becomes a day with a twenty percent chance on the evening broadcast. Nobody is lying, exactly. But a listener who learns over a year that “twenty percent” rarely means rain will reasonably begin to ignore it, and the number stops carrying information at all.

The fix, where it has been tried, is modest. Say what the number refers to, once, plainly, and keep saying it. Some weather services now attach a sentence to their forecasts explaining that the figure refers to the chance of rain at a given place, and some show it alongside an icon rather than instead of one. None of this turns listeners into statisticians. It does not need to. It gives them the one missing piece, the answer to “thirty percent of what?”, without which the number was always going to be filled in by guesswork.

It is tempting to treat this as a small matter, since the cost of misreading a rain forecast is usually a wet sleeve. But the same structure appears wherever a probability is handed to someone who must act on it: the chance that a medication causes a side effect, the chance that a river floods a town, the chance that a bridge needs repair before the next inspection. In each case, the number is only as useful as the listener’s understanding of what it is a number of. Forecasters, because they speak to millions of people every day, simply found this out first.

title: What the Tip Is For
text:
Ask a diner why she leaves a tip and she will usually say that it rewards good service. It is a reasonable belief, and it is the justification the whole custom rests on. It is also, as far as researchers have been able to measure, mostly wrong. When studies compare the size of tips with diners’ own ratings of the service they received, the connection turns out to be real but remarkably weak. How good the service was explains only a small share of why one table leaves more than another.

What explains the rest is less flattering. Tips rise with the size of the bill, which is not a measure of service at all. They rise when the server introduces herself by name, when she crouches beside the table rather than standing over it, and when the weather outside is sunny. They rise, in some studies, with the server’s appearance. A diner who believes she is grading a performance is in fact responding to a scattering of cues, many of which have nothing to do with how well she was served and some of which she would be embarrassed to learn she was responding to. Asked afterward, diners rarely mention any of these. They mention the service.

The custom did not always look inevitable. When tipping spread in the United States in the decades after the Civil War, many Americans regarded it as a European import and an undemocratic one: a way for the wealthy to keep a class of workers dependent on their goodwill. Critics called it a form of bribery, and newspaper columnists and labour organisers alike denounced it. Several states passed laws against it in the years before the First World War. The laws were almost impossible to enforce, and by the late 1920s every one of them had been repealed, but their existence is a reminder that the practice was once argued about rather than assumed.

Defenders of tipping have a real case, and it deserves to be put fairly. For many servers, tips are not a small supplement but most of what they earn, and in a busy restaurant a skilled server can earn more under tipping than a flat wage would pay. Diners, for their part, say they like the sense that they have some say over what happens at the end of a meal. A restaurant that abolishes tipping and raises its prices to pay a fixed wage is asking both groups to give up something they value. Servers themselves are divided, and many who would gain from a fixed wage say they do not want one. Several that have tried it have quietly gone back.

But the case is strongest where it is least about service. The server who does well under tipping does well mainly because she works in a busy, expensive restaurant, not because she is better at her job than the server in a quiet diner across town. And the diner’s sense of control is real chiefly as a feeling. If the size of a tip depends more on the bill and the sunshine than on anything the server did, then the diner is not steering the server’s behaviour in any meaningful way. She is taking part in a ritual that allows her to believe she is.

None of this means tipping should, or will, disappear. Customs survive for reasons that have little to do with whether they do what they claim, and this one is tangled up with wages, prices, and more than a century of habit. What it means is narrower. If a tip is mostly not a reward for service, then arguments about it should stop pretending otherwise. The honest question is not whether diners ought to be able to reward good service. It is who should bear the risk that a server’s income will rise and fall with things nobody controls: the customer, the restaurant, or the server herself.

At present, for the most part, the answer is the server. That may turn out to be a defensible arrangement; there are servers who prefer it, and they are not fools. It is simply not the arrangement most diners believe they are taking part in when they reach for a pen and do the arithmetic at the bottom of the receipt, pleased to have been generous, and certain that they have just told someone how well she did her job.

title: The Street With No Name
text:
Most people who have an address have never thought about where it came from. It seems to belong to the house the way a nose belongs to a face, and writing it on a form requires no more reflection than signing one’s name. But an address is an invention, and a fairly recent one. For most of history, most people lived in places that had no numbers at all, and a large share of the world’s population still does. Even in wealthy countries, rural houses were often known by a family name or the name of a farm well into the twentieth century.

They manage, as people always have. Directions in an unaddressed neighbourhood are given by landmarks and by relationship: the blue gate past the pharmacy, the house of the woman who sells eggs, two turns after the mosque. This works well among neighbours, who share the landmarks and the relationships, and badly for anyone arriving from outside. A delivery driver new to the area may circle for an hour; a clerk in a distant office cannot find the house at all. The difficulty is not that the system fails. It is that it succeeds only for people who already belong.

House numbers came to many European cities in the eighteenth century, and they did not come because residents asked for them. They came because governments wanted to find people: to tax them, to conscript their sons, to lodge soldiers in their homes. A number painted beside a door made a household visible to an official who had never set foot in the street. Residents understood this perfectly well. In some cities, the newly painted numbers were smeared with mud or scraped away almost as soon as they appeared.

It would be easy to tell the story of the address as a story of the state closing its fist, and there is truth in that telling. But it is not the whole truth, and the rest of it matters. An address is also what allows an ambulance to find a house in the dark, what allows a letter to arrive, and what allows a person to open a bank account, register to vote, or prove to an employer that she lives where she says she does. In parts of the world where many people lack addresses, the lack is felt less as freedom from the state than as exclusion from almost everything that the state and the market offer. Being hard to find is a protection. It is also a cost, and it is usually the poor who pay it.

Recent efforts to extend addressing have tried to take account of both halves of this history. Some cities have organised residents to name their own streets, on the reasoning that a name chosen in a meeting is less likely to be scraped off a wall than one handed down from an office. Other schemes skip streets altogether and divide the whole surface of the earth into small squares, giving each one a short code, so that a house can be located without anyone having to decide what the lane outside it is called. Some residents like the squares for exactly the reasons their designers intended; others distrust a code they did not choose and cannot easily say aloud. These systems are clever. Whether they are trusted is a different question, and it is not one that cleverness answers.

What the history suggests is that the technical problem of addressing was always the easier half. Numbering houses is simple; numbering them in a way that residents accept is not. Where an address has been imposed by people who wanted something from those who lived there, residents have treated it as a form of surveillance and resisted it accordingly. Where it has arrived alongside something residents wanted, such as a sewer line, a postal service, or a legal title to the land under their homes, it has usually been welcomed, and the numbers have sometimes been painted on the walls by the residents themselves.

The number beside a front door, then, is not simply a label. It is the visible end of a long negotiation between people and the institutions that want to reach them, and the terms of that negotiation are still being settled across much of the world. The next time you write your address on a form without a second thought, it may be worth remembering that in another century, on another street, a neighbour might have been out that same night with a bucket of mud.

title: In Defense of the Footnote
text:
Few features of a serious book are as easy to mock as the footnote. It interrupts. It sends the eye plunging to the bottom of the page and back up again, often to learn nothing more than the title of an article in a journal the reader will never see. Publishers of books meant for a general audience have been banishing footnotes for decades, first to the back of the book as endnotes and then, increasingly, to a website, where they may as well not exist. Few readers seem to miss them.

I want to suggest that they should. The footnote is not an ornament attached to an argument after the fact. It is the place where the argument admits what it depends on. A sentence in the body of a history book says that something happened; the note beneath it says how the writer knows, and therefore how the reader could find out whether the writer is wrong. Remove the note and the sentence does not become cleaner. It becomes an assertion that asks to be taken on trust.

This is not a small difference. Every field that deals in evidence, from history to law to medicine, depends on the possibility of checking. A claim that cannot be traced to its source cannot be tested, and a claim that cannot be tested can only be believed or disbelieved, which is to say argued about by temperament rather than by evidence. A court that cited no earlier case, or a medical paper that named no trial, would not be taken seriously for a moment; a popular history that does the same is often praised for its readability. The footnote, for all its fussiness, is a small public commitment: here is where I got this, and you are welcome to go and look.

It is also, at its best, a place of unexpected life. The eighteenth-century historian Edward Gibbon used his notes to argue with other scholars, to confess doubts he did not want in his main text, and to make jokes that would have been out of place in his stately paragraphs. Readers of his history of Rome have long said that the notes are where they come to know him. A footnote can hold the qualification that would clutter a sentence, the counterexample the writer cannot yet explain, the credit owed to someone whose idea made the chapter possible. The main text speaks in one voice. The notes let a second voice speak underneath it.

None of this is to deny that the form is abused. Some writers use notes as a display case, piling up references to prove they have read everything, as though the length of a bibliography were a measure of the strength of an argument. Others use them to hide what they would rather not defend in daylight, burying the one damaging source in small type where it can later be pointed to but will rarely be read. Notes of this kind are not evidence of care; they are a performance of it. A reader is right to be suspicious of notes that run longer than the text they support. The footnote is a tool, and tools can be used badly.

But the case against bad footnotes is not a case against footnotes, any more than a misleading chart is an argument against charts. And the alternative now common in popular books is worse than the abuse it was meant to cure. A book whose sources are listed on a website, or not at all, has not become more honest by becoming less cluttered. It has simply made its debts harder to inspect, and it has gained, though this is rarely said, a writer who knows that fewer readers will check. The reader gains a smoother page and loses the means of disagreeing with it on any grounds other than a hunch.

I do not expect footnotes to return to the bestseller list, and I would not wish every popular book to read like a legal brief. But the next time a small raised number sends your eye to the bottom of the page, it may be worth reading the note as what it is: a writer telling you exactly where to push if you think the argument will not hold. Most writers, most of the time, would rather you did not push. The ones who show you where anyway deserve some credit for it.

title: The Staircase Nobody Noticed
text:
Of all the parts of a building, the staircase may be the one we use most intimately and notice least. We look at façades and ceilings; we choose houses for their light and their kitchens. But we climb stairs with our bodies rather than our eyes, and a good stair asks so little of our attention that we forget we are using it at all. Few visitors to a great building remember its stairs unless they stumbled on them. It is only when a stair is wrong that we discover how much it had been doing.

Architects have known this for a long time. In the late seventeenth century the French architect François Blondel proposed a rule that is still, in one form or another, written into building codes: twice the height of a step plus its depth should equal the length of an ordinary stride. The rule is a statement about the human body rather than about stone or timber. A step that is steeper must be shallower, and a step that is lower must be deeper, because the leg that climbs it has one natural length of stride, and a stair that fights that length will be felt in the knees long before it is understood by the mind.

What the rule does not capture is the stair’s most surprising feature, which is that we stop looking at it. Studies of people climbing and descending stairs have found that walkers glance at the first few steps and then, having taken their measure, look away. The body assumes that every step to come will be like the ones it has just taken, and it moves on that assumption, lifting the foot to a height it has learned rather than one it sees. This is why building codes in many countries allow the height of steps in a single flight to vary by no more than a few millimetres. A step that differs from its neighbours by less than the thickness of a finger can send a person sprawling, not because it is hard to climb, but because nobody was watching it.

Seen this way, a staircase is less a structure than a promise, and its chief virtue is consistency. That is a strange thing to say about an object that has also been, for much of architectural history, a stage. The grand staircases of European palaces were built to be seen: broad, shallow flights that turned and divided so that a guest ascending them could be watched from the landings above, and a host descending them could make an entrance. Their steps were often made deliberately low, which slowed the climber to a stately pace and gave a long gown time to follow. The stair was choreography.

It would be easy to set these two traditions against each other, the humble stair that disappears beneath our feet and the theatrical stair that insists on being admired. But the grand staircase worked on the same principle as the humble one. Its low, deep steps obeyed the same relation between height and stride; they simply chose a slower stride. And its effect depended entirely on the climber not having to think. A guest who had to watch her feet on a palace stair could not make an entrance on it. The theatre was possible only because the stair, underneath the marble, kept its promise.

Modern buildings have tended to hide their stairs, placing them in fire-resistant shafts behind heavy doors and leaving the lifts to carry most people most of the time. There are good reasons for this, and I would not want to climb forty floors for the sake of architectural pleasure. Many office workers could not say where the stairs in their own building are. But something has been lost. A staircase is one of the few places in a building where the design meets the body directly, step by step, and a building that tucks its stairs out of sight has given up one of its best chances to be felt as well as seen.

Architecture is usually praised for what it shows us. The next time you climb a flight of stairs without thinking about it, it may be worth pausing on the landing to notice that you did not have to think. Someone measured your stride before you arrived, and measured it closely enough that you never had to. The quietest part of their work is the part you just used.

title: The Song That Would Not Stay Put
text:
When the American scholar Francis James Child set out in the nineteenth century to collect the traditional ballads of England and Scotland, he met a problem he had not quite expected. The ballads would not hold still. He gathered 305 of them in the end, but for many he printed not one text but a dozen or more, because each singer, and sometimes the same singer on different days, sang the song differently. Child spent decades on the work, corresponding with collectors across Britain and beyond. A ballad might be set in a forest in one version and beside a river in another. A lover’s name changed; a verse vanished; an ending turned from grief to revenge.

For a long time, collectors treated this as decay. Somewhere, they assumed, there had been an original, composed by a single poet and perfect in its way, and each generation of singers had worn a little more off it, like a coin passed from hand to hand. The collector’s task was to recover the original by comparing the damaged copies, much as a scholar of ancient texts compares manuscripts to reconstruct a lost book. Some collectors went further and quietly improved the texts they printed, smoothing a rough line or restoring a rhyme, in the belief that they were repairing the damage rather than adding to it. Variation was evidence of loss.

That view did not survive contact with the singers themselves. In the years around the First World War, the English collector Cecil Sharp travelled through the southern Appalachian mountains and found people singing ballads that their ancestors had carried from Britain more than a century before. The songs had changed. Lords and ladies had become farmers; castles had become cabins; a tune had slowed or quickened to suit a new way of singing. But they had not decayed. They were, if anything, more alive than the versions Sharp knew from books, because they were still doing the work songs do: being sung, by particular people, to particular listeners, about lives those listeners recognised.

It is a mistake, then, to hear every change as damage. A singer who replaces a castle with a cabin is not forgetting the song. She is translating it into a world her listeners live in, and in doing so she keeps it from becoming a museum piece. The folk song is not a text that has been badly copied. It is closer to a recipe that every cook adjusts, or a joke that every teller times differently, and its survival depends on precisely that freedom. The listeners who first heard the cabin version did not hear a lesser song. They heard their own.

This is not to say that nothing is ever lost. Some changes are simple mishearings, words that a singer did not understand and replaced with something that sounded similar but meant nothing. Some verses drop out because they were hard to remember, not because anyone judged them unnecessary, and a story can be left with a gap in it that nobody notices anymore. A defender of the folk process who claims that every variant is an improvement is being as sentimental as the collector who claimed that every variant was a ruin. Change is not always growth. It is simply what happens to a song that is still in use.

The surprise is what happened next. Once songs could be printed cheaply and, later, recorded, the variation began to slow. A singer who learns a ballad from a record learns one version, sung the same way every time, and is likely to reproduce it faithfully, as she would a poem memorised from a page. Recording, the very technology that allowed collectors to preserve the living tradition, also gave it a single fixed form to be measured against. A version that departed from the record began to sound less like a variant and more like a mistake.

Nobody intended this, and it is not entirely to be regretted; the recordings preserve voices and styles that would otherwise have vanished. But it is worth noticing that the old collectors got their wish in the end. The songs have, to a large extent, stopped changing. The price was that they have also, to a large extent, stopped being folk songs in the old sense, and become something closer to what the collectors always thought they were: texts, with authors, to be performed correctly.

title: The Land That Is Still Rising
text:
In 1731 the Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius, now remembered mainly for his temperature scale, had a line cut into a rock on a small island in the Gulf of Bothnia to mark the level of the sea. He was trying to settle a question that fishermen and farmers along that coast had been asking for generations. Rocks that their grandparents had sailed around were now islands; islands had become hills joined to the shore; harbours that had served towns for centuries were growing too shallow for boats. Celsius, like most scholars of his day, concluded that the water of the Baltic was slowly draining away.

He was right about the measurement and wrong about the cause. The sea was not falling. The land was rising, and it is rising still: along the northern coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, by nearly a centimetre a year, fast enough that a person who lives there for a lifetime can see the shoreline move. Along some stretches of that coast, a jetty built by one generation must be extended by the next simply to reach the water. The cause lies not in the present but in the last ice age, which ended in that region roughly ten thousand years ago.

At its greatest extent, the ice sheet that covered Scandinavia was in places more than two kilometres thick. Ice is heavy, and a sheet of it that thick presses down on the crust beneath with a weight that is difficult to imagine. The crust responded by sinking. It could sink because the rock of the mantle below it, though solid, is not rigid over long periods of time: under steady pressure it flows, very slowly, the way cold pitch or glacier ice itself will flow if given long enough. The mantle beneath Scandinavia was squeezed outward, and the land settled several hundred metres lower than it would otherwise have stood.

When the ice melted, the weight was removed almost at once, geologically speaking. The land began to rebound. It rose quickly at first and has been slowing ever since, but it has not finished, because the mantle that must flow back beneath it moves at a pace measured in thousands of years. In a sense, the ground of northern Sweden and Finland still remembers the ice and is still recovering from it. By some estimates it has tens of metres of rising yet to do. Satellite measurements now track the rise from year to year, and they agree closely with the marks cut in the old rocks.

The same process is under way wherever great ice sheets once lay: around Hudson Bay in Canada, where old beaches now stand in staircases far above the present shore, and in Scotland, which is rising more slowly. What is less widely known is that it has a counterpart. When the ice pressed the land beneath it down, the displaced mantle pushed up a broad bulge in the land around the edges of the ice sheet, much as pressing a thumb into a soft cushion raises the fabric around it. With the ice gone, those bulges are subsiding. Parts of the Netherlands, southern England, and the eastern coast of the United States are sinking, in part for this reason, while the lands that bore the ice rise.

This matters more than it might seem. Along coasts that are rising, the sea level measured against the land is falling, even as the oceans themselves grow higher; in parts of the Gulf of Bothnia the ground is still winning the race. Along coasts that sit on a sinking bulge, the two effects add together, and a town there faces a faster rise of the sea than the global average would suggest. Planners who read only the global figure may be preparing for the wrong future in both places.

Celsius’s mark is still there on its rock, now well above the water line, along with later marks cut by those who came to check it. The rock did not move in any way that anyone standing on it could feel. It has simply been carried upward, a little each year, by a slow rebound from a weight that lifted before the first farmers arrived. It is a useful reminder that the ground beneath us, which we treat as the fixed stage on which everything else happens, is itself still responding to events that ended long ago.

title: A Memory for Ten Thousand Places
text:
Every autumn in the high mountains of western North America, a grey, crow-sized bird called the Clark’s nutcracker sets about a task that seems, on paper, impossible. Over a few weeks it harvests the seeds of pine trees, carries them off in a pouch beneath its tongue that can hold dozens of seeds at a time, and buries them in small caches of a few seeds each, scattered over many square kilometres of slope. A single bird may bury tens of thousands of seeds in several thousand separate places. Then, over the following winter and spring, it comes back and digs most of them up again.

It does this by memory. For a long time that claim was met with scepticism, and the scepticism was reasonable. Perhaps the birds simply searched likely spots and found seeds by smell, or by chance, or by spotting the disturbed soil of a cache. Each of these explanations was tested, and each failed. In laboratory experiments, nutcrackers allowed to cache seeds in a room floored with sand returned to their own cache sites far more accurately than chance would allow, and they found caches made by other birds in the same room no better than chance. They were not smelling seeds or reading the sand. They were remembering where they had put them. Some studies suggest that they even remember which caches they have already emptied.

What they remember, it turns out, is geometry. When researchers moved the objects in the room, such as stones and pieces of wood, the birds searched in places that bore the same relation to the landmarks as their caches had, shifted by just the amount the landmarks had been shifted. They had not memorised the spot itself so much as its position among the things around it, and they seem to rely most on landmarks close to the cache. In the wild, where snow can bury the ground but not the boulders and trees, this is exactly the kind of memory a bird would need.

The nutcracker’s brain reflects the demand. The hippocampus, a region involved in spatial memory in birds as in mammals, is larger in nutcrackers and other hoarding birds than in related species that do not store food. It would be too simple to say that the bird has a better memory in general; in tests of other kinds of memory, nutcrackers do not stand out. What they have is a memory specialised for one problem, shaped by thousands of generations in which a bird that could not find its seeds did not survive the winter.

The trees have a stake in this too. The whitebark pine, one of the nutcracker’s main sources of food, produces large, wingless seeds in cones that do not open on their own. The wind cannot spread them. Many other pines have winged seeds that ride the wind; the whitebark has given up that option and staked its future on the bird. The nutcracker can, and for the whitebark pine it is close to the only disperser that matters. Seeds that the bird buries and never returns for are left in just the conditions a seedling needs, shallow soil on open ground, and a good number of them grow.

It is tempting to describe this as a happy accident: the bird forgets some of its caches, and the forgotten seeds become the next generation of trees. But that gets the story backward. The nutcracker does not forget much. It caches more seed than it will need, because a winter can be longer than expected and because some caches will be raided by squirrels or lost to other mishaps. The surplus is insurance, and the forest grows from the insurance, not from failures of memory. A bird with a poorer memory would need to bury even more, and a pine that relied on forgetfulness would be relying on a very unreliable partner.

That partnership is now under strain. Whitebark pine has been declining across much of its range, struck by an introduced fungal disease, by beetles, and by a warming climate that lets competing trees climb higher up the slopes. Where the pines grow scarce, nutcrackers leave to feed elsewhere, and the seeds that remain are less likely to be carried off and planted. A tree that depends on a bird’s memory depends, in the end, on the bird being there to remember. In some places, conservation workers have begun planting disease-resistant whitebark seedlings by hand, doing slowly and expensively what the bird once did for nothing.

title: The Uses of a Fever
text:
Few symptoms are treated with as much suspicion as a fever. A parent who finds a child hot to the touch reaches for a thermometer and then, often, for a bottle of medicine, and the number on the thermometer is watched as though it were the illness itself. It is not. A fever is something the body does, not something that is done to it, and the question of whether to fight it depends on understanding what it is for.

The body’s temperature is held steady by a region of the brain that works much like the thermostat in a house. During an infection, chemical signals released by the immune system reach that region and change its setting. The body then behaves as it would in a cold room: blood vessels near the skin narrow, muscles begin to shiver, and the person feels chilled even as their temperature climbs. The shivering is not a sign that something has gone wrong with the thermostat. It is the thermostat working, at a new setting the body has chosen. It is also why a fever often ends in sweating: when the setting drops back, the body finds itself too warm for its thermostat and works to shed the extra heat.

Why would the body choose it? Raising the temperature of an entire body by a couple of degrees is expensive; each degree increases the rate at which energy is burned by roughly ten percent. Evolution does not usually preserve costly responses that do nothing. And the evidence suggests that fever does do something. Many of the cells of the immune system work faster at fever temperatures, moving more quickly toward an infection and multiplying more readily, while some bacteria and viruses reproduce less well when the body around them is warmer. During an infection the body also withdraws iron, which many bacteria need in order to multiply, from the blood, making itself a poorer place for them to grow.

The most striking evidence comes from animals that cannot make a fever the way we do. Lizards generate little heat of their own; they warm themselves by moving into the sun and cool themselves by retreating into shade. In experiments in the 1970s, lizards infected with bacteria moved to warmer parts of their enclosures than healthy lizards chose, raising their body temperature by several degrees through behaviour alone. When researchers kept infected lizards from reaching the warmer spots, more of them died. Fish and even some insects have since been found to do the same thing, seeking out warmth when they are sick. A response that turns up in animals so distantly related, achieved by such different means, is unlikely to be an accident.

None of this means that every fever should be left alone. Very high temperatures can be dangerous in themselves, and some people, such as those with certain heart conditions, may not be able to afford the extra strain a fever imposes. A sick child who cannot sleep or drink because she feels so wretched may recover better with some relief than without it. Medicine that lowers a fever also eases aches, and comfort is not a trivial goal. Doctors who recommend treating a fever for these reasons are not ignoring the science. They are weighing it.

What the evidence does not support is the reflex that treats the fever as the enemy. Studies that have tried to measure whether lowering a fever lengthens an illness have produced mixed results: some find a small effect, many find none, and the question remains open. That uncertainty cuts both ways. It means there is no strong case for suppressing every fever, but also no strong case for enduring a miserable one out of principle. The number on the thermometer, taken alone, tells a parent less than how the child is eating, drinking, and behaving. Nurses tell parents this constantly, and parents, watching the number climb, often do not believe them.

It is worth remembering that the fever and the infection, though they arrive together, are on opposite sides. When we bring the temperature down, we are not weakening the illness. We are overruling a decision the body has made, sometimes for good reasons of our own. The lizard crawling toward a warm rock, sick and with no medicine to take, is doing the only thing it can, and it turns out to be the same thing our own bodies were doing all along.

title: Two Views on the Wolves of Yellowstone
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by an ecologist. Passage B is adapted from an article by a wildlife biologist. Both concern the effects of returning wolves to Yellowstone National Park.
text:
PASSAGE A

In the winter of 1995, fourteen grey wolves captured in Canada were released into Yellowstone National Park, where wolves had been absent for some seventy years; more followed the next year. What happened next has become one of the best-known stories in ecology. With wolves hunting them, the elk that had crowded the park’s river valleys grew fewer and warier. They spent less time browsing on the young willows and aspens along the streams, and in places those trees began to grow tall again for the first time in decades. Songbirds returned to the thickets. Beavers, finding willow to eat and build with, came back to some streams.

The name for this pattern is a trophic cascade: a change at the top of a food chain that tumbles down through the levels below it. Ecologists had described cascades before, in lakes and tide pools, but Yellowstone offered one on the scale of a landscape, and it carried a message that reached far beyond the park. Predators are not merely consumers of prey. They shape where prey animals go and how they behave, and through that behaviour they shape the plants and even the rivers. In one widely shared telling, the wolves changed the course of rivers themselves, as steadier banks and returning trees narrowed and deepened the channels.

It is fair to say that the story has sometimes been told too neatly, as though wolves alone had redrawn the map of the park. But its core holds. Where wolves returned, the pressure on streamside trees eased, and recovery followed. For a century, the killing of large predators was treated as a matter of protecting livestock and game. Yellowstone suggests that it was also the removal of a force that had been holding whole ecosystems in their shape, and that returning such a force can begin to restore what its absence undid. Critics who point to other causes are right that other things changed as well; they are wrong if they conclude that the wolves were a bystander.

PASSAGE B

The wolves of Yellowstone have become a parable, and parables are hard to argue with. That is exactly why the evidence deserves a second look. The elk population of the park’s northern range did fall steeply after wolves returned, but wolves were not the only change. Hunters were killing many elk that wandered outside the park in those same years, a run of droughts reduced the forage available, and grizzly bears and cougars, whose numbers were also rising, were taking many elk calves. Untangling the wolves’ share from all of this is difficult, and estimates vary widely. A pack of wolves chasing elk across a snowy valley is a vivid image; a table of hunting permits is not, and the table matters too.

The claim that elk began avoiding the valleys out of fear has proved harder still to confirm. When researchers fitted elk with tracking collars, they found that the animals did not, on the whole, shun the places where wolves were most likely to hunt. Elk, it seems, are more practical than the parable allows: they go where the food is, and they take their chances. The simpler explanation for any recovery of the trees is that there were fewer elk eating them. And the recovery itself has been patchier than popular accounts suggest. Some stands of willow have grown tall; many have not.

One reason is the beavers. During the decades without wolves, heavy browsing by elk stripped away much of the willow, the beavers that depended on it disappeared, and without beaver dams to hold water in the valleys, the streams cut deeper channels and the water table fell. A willow growing beside a stream that now runs a metre lower than it once did may never reach the water it needs, however few elk are eating it. The ecosystem did not simply wait for the wolves to return. It changed into something else in their absence, and removing the cause has not undone all of the effects. Some researchers have begun building beaver dams by hand in an effort to raise the water again.

None of this means the wolves have done nothing. It means that restoring a predator is not the same as rewinding a clock. The wolves are part of the story, and perhaps an important part. They are not the whole of it, and a story that makes them the whole of it will mislead the next park that hopes to repeat the trick.

title: Two Views on Finishing an Unfinished Novel
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by a novelist. Passage B is adapted from an essay by a literary scholar. Both concern novels that their authors left unfinished when they died.
text:
PASSAGE A

When Charles Dickens died in 1870, he left behind half of a novel, The Mystery of Edwin Drood, and a mystery in the literal sense: nobody knew what had become of Edwin. Within a few years other writers had begun to supply endings, and they have not stopped since. Some of these completions are clumsy; a few are ingenious. One was produced by a man who claimed that Dickens had dictated it to him from beyond the grave, which is at least a novel theory of authorship. I have read perhaps a dozen, and I do not regret any of them, because each one took the book seriously enough to argue with it.

I think of finishing another writer’s book as a conversation carried on after one of the speakers has left the room. It is not a forgery. Nobody who picks up a completed novel is fooled about who wrote which part; the join is announced on the cover and is usually visible on the page. What the completion offers is a reading: one writer’s best guess, made in the only form a novelist has, about where the story was going. Critics offer such guesses in essays all the time. A novelist offers them in chapters. A good completion shows its reasoning the way a good essay does, in clues picked up and threads carried forward.

The usual objection is that the dead writer cannot consent. That is true, and it is also true of almost everything that happens to a book after its author dies: it is edited, abridged, translated, adapted for the stage, taught badly in schools. Books are not kept pure by their authors’ deaths. They are kept alive by being used. An unfinished novel left untouched in an archive is honoured in the way a sealed tomb is honoured, and read about as often.

I would not want every fragment completed, and I would not want a completion to replace the fragment on the shelf. But a story that stops in the middle is a kind of invitation, and some of the best readers a book will ever have are the ones who accept it. An invitation can be declined, and most readers will decline this one. Those who accept it should be allowed to show their work.

PASSAGE B

Franz Kafka asked his friend Max Brod to burn his unfinished manuscripts after his death. Brod refused and published them instead, and the world gained The Trial and The Castle. It is hard to wish he had obeyed. But it is worth noticing what Brod did not do. He did not write the missing chapters. He arranged what Kafka had left, made editorial choices that scholars still dispute, and let the books end where Kafka’s pen had stopped. Readers of The Castle know that it breaks off in the middle of a sentence, and that knowledge has become part of the book.

This is the distinction I want to defend. Publishing an unfinished work is an act of preservation: it puts before readers everything the writer actually wrote, gaps included. Completing it is an act of replacement, however modestly it is presented. A reader who finishes a completed novel does not experience the book the writer left. She experiences a story with an ending, and endings do not stay politely in their own chapters. They reach back and change the meaning of everything that came before. A mystery is only the most obvious case; the ending of any book tells us what kind of book it was. A completed Edwin Drood is not half a Dickens novel and half someone else’s; it is, in effect, a new book whose first half happens to have been written by Dickens.

Defenders of completion say that it is only one reading among many, and that the fragment remains available to anyone who wants it. In principle, yes. In practice, the completed version is the one that gets printed in paperback, adapted for television, and remembered. The fragment, which was the thing the author actually made, becomes a curiosity for scholars. Television does not adapt fragments.

Nobody would carve the missing arms onto an ancient statue and call the result the statue. An unfinished book is incomplete, but it is not defective. Its unfinishedness is a fact about it, as much as its setting and its characters are, and a reader deserves to meet that fact rather than be protected from it.

title: The Clock in the Window
text:
I took the job at Havel’s Watch and Clock Repair because it was the only shop on Dorset Street with a sign in the window that said HELP WANTED and did not also say MUST BE 18. I was sixteen, and I had pictured something from a film: a hunched old man with a jeweller’s loupe screwed into one eye, passing on the secrets of his trade to a gifted apprentice. The loupe turned out to be accurate. The rest of the picture did not. For the first three weeks, the secrets that Mr. Havel passed on to me concerned the broom, the correct way to wrap a mantel clock in newspaper, and the fact that the kettle in the back room was never to be filled above the line.

The shop was a single narrow room lined with clocks, perhaps sixty of them, and every one of them was running. They did not agree with one another. A few ran a minute fast and a few a minute slow, so that on the hour the room went off like a slow, uneven round of applause that could take most of a minute to die away. Mr. Havel said he could tell by ear which clocks needed attention, and I assumed he was showing off until the afternoon he stopped in the middle of a sentence, walked to a walnut wall clock by the door, listened, and said, “That one is tired.” Its owner came for it a week later and was told that the mainspring had been about to go.

The exception was the clock in the front window. It was a large brass carriage clock on a velvet stand, the handsomest thing in the shop, and its hands stood at ten past four. They had stood at ten past four since before I arrived, and nobody wound it. I decided, in the way a sixteen-year-old decides things, that there was a tragedy behind it. Someone had died at ten past four. A wife, probably. I built the whole story in an afternoon and was quietly moved by it, and for several days I was careful never to dust that clock, in case the gesture was too much for him.

It was a customer who asked, in the end. She had come in with a wristwatch that had stopped, and on her way out she pointed at the window and said, not unkindly, that a watchmaker ought to be able to fix his own clock. Mr. Havel smiled at her the way he smiled at a clock that was keeping perfect time. When she had gone, I asked him gently whether it was hard to talk about. He looked at me with great interest, as though I had just told him something surprising about myself.

“It is the best clock in the shop,” he said. “Every day, people walk past that window and see the wrong time. And what do they do?” He waited, and when I did not answer he raised his wrist and looked at it. They check their own watches, he said. Some of them notice, for the first time in months, that their watch is running slow, or that it has stopped altogether. “A clock that is right, nobody looks at twice. A clock that is wrong, everybody checks against. Half of my repairs come in through that window.”

I would like to say that I was delighted to have the mystery solved. In fact I was annoyed, and a little embarrassed, and for the rest of the afternoon I swept with more energy than the floor required. There had been no wife. There had been, as far as I could ever discover, no tragedy of any kind in Mr. Havel’s life beyond a long dispute with his landlord about the drains. I had been sentimental on his behalf, and he had been, the whole time, running a business.

He did teach me some repair work, eventually, toward the end of August: how to open a case back without scarring it, how to lift a balance wheel with tweezers and hold my breath while doing it. I was not especially good at it. What stayed with me instead was the window. I have worked in several offices since, and in every one of them I have noticed that people argue hardest against a figure that is obviously wrong and pay no attention at all to one that is only slightly off. I have occasionally, I admit, left an obvious mistake in a draft on purpose, just to see who would stop and check their watch.

title: Holding the Ladder
text:
My sister Maren announced in May that she would repaint the house before she left for university, and that I would help her, and she said both of these things in the same tone, as though they were equally settled facts about the weather. I was fourteen. I had plans for the summer that involved a great deal of lying down. I pointed out that our parents had not asked anyone to repaint the house. Maren pointed out that the north wall had been flaking since I was in primary school, which was true, and that she had already bought the paint, which was worse.

My job, it turned out, was the ladder. Maren did the scraping and the priming and the painting; I stood at the bottom with both hands on the rails and one foot on the lowest rung, and I held it. That was all. For the first few days I considered this an insult. Anyone could hold a ladder. A fence post could hold a ladder. I said so, several times, and Maren, from somewhere above my head, said that a fence post would at least not keep talking.

She was unbearable about the work. She scraped every board down to bare wood, even where the old paint was sound, because, she said, new paint over old paint was only as good as the old paint. She would not paint in direct sun, because the paint dried too fast and left lap marks, so we worked our way around the house in a slow circle that followed the shade: the west wall in the morning, the east wall in the afternoon. When a brush hair came loose in a wet stroke, she stopped everything to pick it out with a pin. At that rate, I calculated, we would finish the house at about the time she graduated.

The morning I understood the ladder was the morning it slipped. We were on the west side, where the ground slopes toward the garden, and I had taken my foot off the rung to swat at a wasp. The feet of the ladder slid perhaps three inches on the damp grass. Nothing else happened. Maren caught the gutter, I grabbed the rails, and the ladder stopped. But I looked up and saw her, twenty feet above me, holding a full can of paint in one hand and the edge of the roof in the other, and she looked down at me and did not say anything at all, which from Maren was the loudest thing possible.

After that I held the ladder as though it were the whole job, which I suppose it was. I learned to test the ground before she climbed, to set the feet on a board when the grass was wet, to lean my weight in when she reached sideways. I stopped talking so much. I started, without meaning to, to watch what she was doing up there, and to notice when a stroke was too thin or the edge along a window frame was not quite straight. Once I pointed one out. She looked at it, frowned, and fixed it, and neither of us mentioned it again.

We finished on the twenty-ninth of August, three days before she left. The house was pale grey, the colour of a pigeon, and the neighbours said kind things about it, and my father walked all the way around it twice without speaking, which in our family is a standing ovation. Maren took one photograph of it from the road and did not seem especially interested in looking at it after that. I think the finished house mattered to her less than the way it had been done.

Two summers later the shed needed painting, and there was no ladder to hold, because the shed is only eight feet tall. I scraped it down to bare wood, all of it, including the boards where the old paint was perfectly sound. I followed the shade around it. When a brush hair came loose I went into the kitchen for a pin. My mother, watching from the window, asked me who I was trying to impress, and I told her nobody, which was true, and which was also, I realised as I said it, exactly the answer Maren would have given.

title: Waiting on the Ice
text:
My uncle Ansel does not believe in conversation before nine in the morning, and on the lake he does not believe in it much after nine either. I learned this on the first day of the week I spent with him in February, the winter my parents were, as they put it, “sorting some things out,” and decided that I would be better off sorting nothing out a hundred and fifty miles to the north. I was fifteen, and I had never been anywhere so cold that the inside of my nose froze when I breathed. Ansel handed me a pair of insulated boots two sizes too large, a thermos, and an auger, and walked out onto the lake without looking back to see whether I was following.

Ice fishing, I can now report, consists of drilling a hole in a frozen lake, dropping a line into it, and then sitting on an overturned bucket for a length of time that has no upper limit. Ansel had a canvas shelter about the size of a phone booth, with a heater that smelled of burnt dust, and we sat in it side by side, each watching our own hole in the ice as if it might say something. For the first two hours I kept a mental list of everything I would rather be doing. It reached forty-one items, and one of them was going to the dentist.

Then the lake made a sound. It started somewhere far off to my left, a deep, rising note, like someone running a wet finger around the rim of an enormous glass, and it swept under us and away to the right and ended in a crack like a door slamming in an empty house. I was on my feet before it finished. I believe I grabbed Ansel’s arm. He looked at my hand on his sleeve, and then at me, with the mild curiosity of a man who has noticed a bird he does not recognize.

“That’s the ice talking,” he said. When the air gets colder, he explained, the top of the ice shrinks, and the whole sheet, which is miles across and has nowhere to go, cracks and shifts to take up the strain, and the sound runs through it the way sound runs along a railway line. It happens most on cold, clear afternoons, as the temperature drops. He said all this the way other people say it looks like rain. “Loud ice is thick ice,” he said. “It’s got enough to it to sing. The one you want to worry about is the ice that doesn’t say anything, in spring, when it’s gone soft.”

I sat down again. I did not believe him, exactly, but I noticed that he had not moved, and that the heater was still humming, and that the line in his hole had not so much as twitched. The lake spoke again about twenty minutes later, a shorter note this time, and I held on to the edge of my bucket rather than to him, and it passed. By the end of the afternoon I had stopped jumping. By the end of the week I found that I was waiting for it, the way you wait for a particular line in a song.

We caught, in five days, eleven perch, of which Ansel kept four, and I would not describe any of it as exciting. What I remember instead is the long stretches in which neither of us said anything and it did not feel like an argument. At home that winter, silence had meant that something was wrong. Out on the lake it seemed to mean only that nobody had anything to add, and I was surprised by how restful that was, and a little ashamed of the forty-one items.

My parents did sort things out, as it happens, though not in the way I had feared. When my mother picked me up on the Sunday, she asked how the week had gone, and I said it had been fine, and she looked at me carefully, as though trying to tell which kind of quiet it was. I have thought since that Ansel would have understood the question. Some silences are soft and dangerous, and some of them just mean the ice is thick enough to hold you.

title: The Last Speaker Problem
text:
Every few years a newspaper runs the story of a last speaker. An old woman or man, photographed at a kitchen table, is described as the final person on earth who can speak some language, and the article ends with a sentence about a whole way of seeing the world vanishing with them. The stories are moving, and they are meant to be. They also, I think, get the arithmetic of language loss slightly wrong, in a way that matters for what happens next.

Consider the best-known last speaker in the English-speaking world. Tradition holds that the Cornish language died in 1777 with a fish-seller named Dolly Pentreath, who is said to have cursed in it at people who could not understand her. The tradition is almost certainly too tidy. There is evidence that others who spoke some Cornish outlived her, and families in Cornwall went on using Cornish words and phrases, counting rhymes and names for fish and tools, for generations afterward. What died in 1777, if anything did, was a particular kind of speaker: someone who had learned the language first, as a child, and used it for everything. What did not die was a larger and harder-to-count population of people who knew some of it.

That population is the one the last-speaker story leaves out. Linguists who study endangered languages describe a spectrum rather than a line. At one end are fluent speakers who learned the language at home. Next come what are sometimes called semi-speakers, who understand a great deal and can speak some, often haltingly, because they grew up hearing the language but answering in another one. Beyond them are people who know songs, prayers, greetings, and the names of plants. A census that asks only whether someone is a fluent speaker will count the first group and miss the others entirely, and it will record the language’s death on the day the first group reaches zero.

The distinction is not academic. When a language is declared dead, money for teaching it tends to dry up, and families who have kept fragments of it may stop passing them on, reasoning that a dead language is not worth the trouble. The declaration can bring about the thing it describes. Conversely, some of the most striking revivals of recent decades have been built out of exactly the fragments that a count of fluent speakers ignores. Cornish itself is now taught in some schools and spoken by a small number of enthusiasts as a living second language, reconstructed from old texts, from place names, and from the scattered words that families never quite let go.

None of this means that the alarm about language loss is overstated. By most estimates, a large share of the world’s roughly seven thousand languages are no longer being learned by children, and a language that children do not learn will, sooner or later, lose its fluent speakers whether anyone photographs the last of them or not. A revived language is also not the same thing as an unbroken one. The people who learn Cornish today learn it in classrooms, as teenagers or adults, and the language they speak has been rebuilt with modern words and, inevitably, with an accent shaped by English. Some linguists argue that calling it the same language is a kindness rather than a description.

But the more useful question is not whether a language is alive or dead. It is what is left of it, held by whom, and in what form. A community with no fluent speakers but hundreds of people who know the songs, the prayers, and the grammar recorded in an old dictionary is in a very different position from one in which nothing at all survives, and a count that reports zero in both cases is not telling us much. Anyone deciding where to spend the small sums available for teaching endangered languages needs to know the difference, and the fluent-speaker count, taken alone, hides it.

The last-speaker story has one more flaw, which is that it is always told as an ending. The woman at the kitchen table is usually not the end of anything. She is, more often than the headlines allow, the person a grandchild comes to with a notebook, asking how to say the word for the river. Languages have been lost for good before, and some will be again, but whether a particular one is lost depends a great deal on whether anyone thinks to ask.

title: The Scale Nobody Checks
text:
Most of the trust that holds a market together is invisible, and the most invisible part of it is the scale. When you buy a kilogram of rice or a litre of petrol, you almost never check the quantity. You assume that the number on the pump or the label means what it says, and you assume it because, for a very long time and at considerable expense, someone else has been checking on your behalf. The same is true of the scale at the deli counter, the meter in the taxi, and the gauge that tells a delivery company how much fuel it has pumped. Each is a small promise, and each is kept by people the customer never sees.

It was not always so. For most of history, a unit of weight or volume meant whatever a particular town, market, or merchant said it meant. A bushel in one county could be noticeably larger than a bushel in the next, and a trader who bought by the large measure and sold by the small one could make a living from the difference without ever lying about the number. Rulers issued standards and ordered them copied, and those orders were widely ignored, because a standard that nobody inspects is only a suggestion.

What changed things was not the standard but the inspector. Medieval English towns, for instance, fixed the weight that a loaf of bread had to have at a given price and appointed officials to weigh loaves at random; bakers caught selling light could be fined or publicly shamed. The usual explanation of the “baker’s dozen,” thirteen loaves sold as twelve, is that bakers added the extra loaf to stay safely clear of the penalty. The story may be only partly true, but it captures something real: the rule mattered because someone could come round with a scale.

The modern version of that official is the weights-and-measures inspector, a figure so obscure that most people do not know the job exists. Inspectors test petrol pumps, supermarket scales, taxi meters, and the fill levels of packaged goods, and in most places they find that the great majority are accurate. That finding is sometimes used to argue that the inspections are a waste. It is better read the other way. The scales are accurate largely because they are inspected, in the same way that drivers keep to the limit partly because a police car might be waiting around the next bend.

Standardization has its costs, and they are not only financial. When France introduced the metric system in the 1790s, it swept away hundreds of local units that people had used for generations, many of them tied to the practical work of a particular region, and the resistance was considerable; for a time the government even allowed traditional units back into everyday trade. A single system is easier to police, but it can also flatten real differences in how people farm, build, and trade, and the people asked to give up a familiar measure are rarely the ones who designed its replacement.
