There is also a strange twist at the very top of the system. For more than a century, the kilogram was defined as the mass of one particular metal cylinder kept in a vault near Paris. Official copies were compared with it from time to time, and over the decades the copies and the original were found to have drifted apart by amounts on the order of fifty micrograms, roughly the mass of a small grain of sand. Nobody could say which of them had changed, because the original was, by definition, exactly one kilogram. In 2019 the kilogram was redefined in terms of a constant of nature, partly to end that awkward situation.

The drifting cylinder is a good reminder that the problem the inspectors solve never goes away. Every measure, however carefully made, needs something to be checked against and someone to do the checking. We tend to notice the system only when it fails. Most of the time, its success looks like nothing at all: a litre that is a litre, and a customer who does not think to wonder. Nobody writes to the newspaper to report that a petrol pump delivered exactly what it promised, and that silence, rather than any headline, is the measure of how well the system works.

title: The Homework Hour
text:
Few school practices provoke as much argument, or as little agreement, as homework. Parents complain that there is too much of it or too little; teachers complain that it is not done, or copied, or done by the parents; and every few years a school district somewhere announces that it is abolishing homework altogether and is either praised as humane or denounced as soft. Behind the noise sits a question that sounds simple: does homework help students learn? Students, whose evenings are the ones at stake, are rarely asked what they think, although most of them have views.

The research answer is, frustratingly, that it depends, and especially on age. Reviews of the studies, of which there are now a great many, have generally found a modest positive association between homework and achievement for older students, in the later years of secondary school, and a weak one or none at all for young children. One widely repeated rule of thumb suggests about ten minutes a night for each grade level, so that a first-grader does ten minutes and a senior perhaps two hours. The rule has the appeal of simplicity. How much evidence stands behind the exact figure is less clear.

Even the association for older students needs careful handling, for a reason that is easy to miss. If you survey students and ask how long they spend on homework, the ones who report the most time are not always the highest achievers. Sometimes they are the ones who find the material hardest. A student who understands the chemistry finishes the problem set in twenty minutes; a student who is lost spends two hours on it and still gets half of it wrong. A study that simply lines up hours against grades can therefore make homework look useless, or even harmful, when what it has actually measured is who was struggling.

This is why I think the public argument about homework is mostly an argument about the wrong thing. It asks how much, when the better question is what for. Homework that consists of practising a skill the student has already begun to learn, spread over several days rather than crammed into one, seems to do real good; that kind of spaced practice is among the more reliable findings in the study of memory. Homework that asks students to teach themselves something new, alone at a kitchen table, with no one to tell them when they have gone wrong, is much more doubtful. An hour of the first kind and an hour of the second kind are not the same hour.

There is a fair objection to all this, and it concerns fairness itself. Homework happens at home, and homes are not equal. A student with a quiet room, a reliable internet connection, and a parent who remembers algebra has a very different evening from one who shares a bedroom with two siblings and works a shift after school. Critics argue that homework therefore widens the gaps that schools are supposed to narrow, and they are right that it can. Any serious defence of homework has to reckon with this rather than wave it away.

But the answer to that objection is not obviously to abolish homework. It may be to change what homework asks. Short, focused practice that a student can do alone, without special equipment or a parent’s help, is less likely to reward the advantages of a particular home than a sprawling project that assumes a printer, a car to the craft store, and an adult with free evenings. Some schools have also kept libraries and classrooms open after hours so that students can do their homework somewhere other than home, which rather neatly solves part of the problem without abandoning the practice.

None of this will end the argument. Homework is where school reaches into family life, and people will always have strong feelings about that. But the argument would be more useful if it stopped treating homework as a single thing to be measured by the hour, and started asking, of any particular assignment, what it is supposed to do and whether it does it. That is a less satisfying question than whether homework is good or bad, because it cannot be settled once and for all. It has to be asked again of every worksheet.

title: The Typeface You Do Not Notice
text:
The best typeface, a printer once told me, is the one you do not notice. I was nineteen and had just discovered that my word processor offered two hundred fonts, and I was using a good many of them in a single essay. He picked up a page, held it at arm’s length, and said that it looked like a ransom note. Then he handed me a paperback novel, opened it at random, and asked me what typeface it was set in. I had no idea. That, he said, was the point.

The idea is an old one among people who make books. In a lecture given in the 1930s, the typographer Beatrice Warde compared good printing to a wine glass made of perfectly clear crystal. A true lover of wine, she argued, would choose the clear glass over an ornate golden goblet, because the clear glass shows the wine and the gold hides it. Type, in her view, was a vessel for meaning, and the reader should look through it rather than at it. The moment you notice the letters, something has come between you and the words.

I have come to believe she was mostly right, and the evidence is everywhere once you look for it. The typefaces in which most novels, newspapers, and road signs are set were designed with enormous care, and almost none of the people who read them could name them. Their designers worried over the height of a lowercase letter, the width of an o, the tiny gap between an r and an n that keeps them from blurring into an m at small sizes. All of that labour is spent so that nobody will see it. It is one of the few crafts whose greatest success is to go unremarked.

I should admit that the crystal goblet has its limits. Not all type is meant to be read at length. The lettering on a poster, a shop front, or a record sleeve is supposed to be noticed, and a festival poster set in the plain face of a tax form would fail at its one job. Warde’s argument is an argument about reading, about the long, quiet stretches of text in which a reader should forget that there is any type at all. It does not follow that every letter everywhere should aspire to invisibility, and the most delightful lettering I know is anything but invisible.

There is a deeper difficulty too, and it took me longer to see. A typeface feels invisible largely because we are used to it. For centuries, German readers read most of their books in blackletter, the dense, angular type that English speakers now tend to associate with old certificates and heavy-metal album covers. To those readers, blackletter was the clear glass, and the rounder roman type of English and Italian printers could look foreign and oddly thin. Neither was transparent by nature. Each had become transparent through habit, which means that the clear glass is partly something the reader brings, not only something the designer makes.

That does not defeat the argument, but it changes it. The goal of a book typeface is still to disappear, but disappearing is something a typeface does in the company of particular readers at a particular time, and it can be learned. When a new face is introduced, readers often dislike it for a while and complain that it is ugly or hard to read, and then, a few years later, stop noticing it at all. The complaint and the silence are both evidence of the same thing: the letters had to be looked at before they could be looked through.

I still think of the printer when I choose a typeface, which I do more often than I would have expected at nineteen. I no longer use two hundred of them. I usually pick one of perhaps three, all of them dull, and I am pleased when a reader tells me they enjoyed an essay without mentioning how it looked. The printer would have called that the highest compliment available. I have come to agree, with one reservation: the glass is only clear to eyes that have learned to see through it.

title: The Prompter’s Box
text:
In some of the older opera houses of Europe, if you look closely at the front edge of the stage, you can see a small hooded shell rising from the floor, like the lid of a half-open clam. Most of the audience takes it for a piece of the lighting or a quirk of the architecture. It is the prompter’s box, and in many houses there is still a person inside it, crouched below the level of the footlights with a score, following every bar of the performance and ready to feed a singer the next line.

I first sat in one as a student, during a summer spent doing odd jobs at a small opera festival, and I have never quite recovered from the experience. The box is cramped and hot, and from inside it the stage is a forest of ankles. You cannot see the singers’ faces unless they lean toward you. What you can see is their mouths, when they turn downstage, and after a few nights I found that I could tell from the set of a singer’s jaw, a fraction of a second before an entrance, whether she knew what came next. The prompter I was assisting, a woman who had done the job for thirty years, could tell from their shoulders.

The spoken theatre abandoned the prompter’s box long ago in most places, and there are good reasons it did. Actors who know that someone below them holds the text may learn their lines less thoroughly; a whisper from the box can carry to the front rows; and the whole arrangement belongs to an era when companies staged a new play every week or two and no actor could be expected to know them all. When runs grew longer and rehearsal periods grew with them, the box began to look like a crutch. Most directors I have worked with would regard an actor who needed prompting on opening night as unprepared, and they would be right.

Opera kept the box for reasons that are partly practical. A singer may carry dozens of roles in several languages, sometimes stepping into a production at a day’s notice, and must sing them over an orchestra, while watching a conductor, while moving through staging that may have been rehearsed only briefly. In many houses the prompter does more than rescue forgotten words. She gives entrances, mouthing the first syllable of each phrase just ahead of time, and she relays the conductor’s beat to singers who cannot see it from where they stand. Some singers say that they barely need her. Others admit, privately, that they would not go on without her.

What interests me about the box, though, is less its usefulness than what it admits. Most of the arts present their finished products as though they had arrived whole. A novel does not show you its drafts; a painting rarely shows you the figures the painter scraped away. The prompter’s box is a permanent, visible acknowledgment, built into the stage itself, that the performance you are watching might fail at any moment and that someone has been placed there to catch it. It is the theatre’s way of admitting that memory is fragile, and that art made by living people in real time is always, a little, improvised.

I do not want to romanticize this. A prompter who is needed too often is a sign that something has gone wrong in rehearsal, and a production that leans on her every night is not a good production. The box is a safety net, and nobody goes to the circus hoping to see the net used. But I have come to think that the net changes the act even when it is never touched. Performers who know that a fall will be caught can attempt more, and the best nights I spent in that hot little shell were ones on which I never said a word, because everyone above me was free to take risks, knowing I was there.

The prompter I assisted told me, on the last night of the festival, that the best compliment she had ever received came from a tenor who had not needed her once in a whole season. He had found her after his final performance and thanked her anyway. She seemed to think this was obvious. It took me several years to understand why.

title: An Essay Is an Attempt
text:
The word essay comes into English from French, in which essai means a trial or an attempt, and the writer usually credited with giving the form its name, Michel de Montaigne, seems to have meant it quite literally. When he published the first books of his Essais in 1580, he was not presenting conclusions. He was trying things out: testing his judgment on subjects as various as cannibals, thumbs, idleness, and the education of children, to see what it would make of them. He admits more than once that he does not know where a given piece will end up when he begins it.

Most students meet the essay in a very different form. The version taught in many schools has five paragraphs: an introduction that ends with a thesis, three body paragraphs that each support it, and a conclusion that restates it. The thesis comes first, the evidence is lined up behind it, and nothing in the piece is allowed to surprise the writer. It is, in a sense, the opposite of an attempt. It is a report of an attempt that was already completed somewhere else, before the writing began. Its conclusion, which often opens with the words “in conclusion,” tells the reader what the reader has just been told three times, and it rarely tells the writer anything at all.

I do not think the five-paragraph essay is useless, and I want to be fair to it before I complain about it. It teaches something real. A student who has never organized an argument learns from it that claims need support, that a reader needs to be told where a piece is going, and that a paragraph should be about one thing. Those are not small lessons, and many adult writers could stand to learn them again. A scaffold is not a building, but you cannot put up most buildings without one.

The trouble begins when the scaffold is mistaken for the building. A student who learns that an essay must know its conclusion before it starts learns, by implication, that writing is not a way of thinking but a way of displaying thought that is already finished. The essay becomes a container rather than a search. I have read many essays by clever students that were perfectly organized and entirely inert, because the writer had decided what to say in the first ten minutes and spent the next two hours defending a position that had never been at risk.

Montaigne worked differently, and there is a detail of his method that I find more instructive than anything he says about it. He kept revising the Essais for the rest of his life, and his revisions were mostly additions. Rather than cutting what he no longer believed, he tended to write new thoughts into the margins beside the old ones, sometimes qualifying them, sometimes contradicting them outright. Later editors have marked the layers so that a reader can see, on a single page, the younger Montaigne and the older one disagreeing. The result can be maddening to read. It is also an honest record of a mind changing, which a tidy final draft would have hidden.

Nobody should hand in an essay that contradicts itself without noticing. But there is a difference between a contradiction the writer has missed and one the writer has chosen to show, and it is the second kind that school essays almost never allow. The best essays I know, by Montaigne and by the many writers who have followed him, are ones in which the writer can be caught in the act of thinking: starting from one place, meeting a difficulty, and arriving somewhere slightly unexpected, with the route left visible. Readers can follow such a route, and they tend to trust it more than a straight line, because they can see the places where the writer was tempted to turn back.

I am not proposing that schools abandon the five-paragraph essay. I am proposing that they tell students what it is: a set of training wheels, useful for a while, and not the thing itself. The thing itself is an attempt. It is allowed to fail. It is, in fact, only worth reading if it might have.

title: Taste at Arm’s Length
text:
If you hand an octopus a shrimp, it may not look at it. An arm will reach out, the suckers along its underside will close on the shrimp one after another, and the prey will be passed from sucker to sucker toward the mouth in a smooth, rolling motion that resembles nothing so much as a conveyor belt. The animal’s large eyes may be pointed somewhere else entirely. To a human observer, used to thinking of the brain as the place where decisions are made, the scene is faintly unsettling. The arm seems to know what it is doing.

In a sense it does. An octopus has on the order of five hundred million neurons, a number comparable to that of some small mammals, and by most estimates about two-thirds of them are not in the head at all. They are in the arms. Each arm has a thick cord of nerve tissue running along its length, with clusters of neurons near each sucker, and a great deal of the work of reaching, grasping, and handling seems to be done there, locally, with only general instructions coming down from the central brain.

The suckers themselves are more than grips. Each one is lined with thousands of sensory cells, and many of these respond not to pressure but to chemicals. An octopus, in other words, can taste what it touches. Researchers studying these cells have reported that they respond to substances found in prey and to bitter compounds that might signal something unpleasant to eat, and it has been suggested that this is how an octopus hunting blind, with an arm pushed deep into a crevice, can tell a crab from a stone without seeing either. The arm does not merely feel its way. It samples.

The most striking evidence of how independent the arms are comes from experiments that are hard to describe without wincing. When an arm is separated from the animal, which octopuses can survive and eventually regrow, it continues for some time to respond on its own. Touched, it may curl away. Offered a piece of food, it may grasp it and attempt to pass it toward where the mouth would have been. Whatever is guiding these movements, it cannot be the brain, which is no longer attached.

This raises a puzzle that turns out to have a surprising answer. If each arm grabs anything that tastes like food, and an octopus has eight of them, often tangled together, why do the arms not constantly seize one another? One study suggested that the answer lies in the skin. Separated arms, it found, readily grabbed a range of objects but largely avoided grabbing octopus skin, and they grabbed a piece of material coated with an extract of octopus skin less often than the same material left plain. Something in the skin seemed to tell the suckers, in effect, that this was not food but self. The researchers also noticed that a living octopus would sometimes ignore the rule and handle a severed arm as though it were prey, which suggests that the central brain can overrule the arms’ local chemistry when it chooses to.

It is tempting to describe this as an animal with nine brains, one central and one in each arm, and the phrase appears often in popular writing. Most researchers would regard it as an exaggeration. The arms are not independent minds; they are coordinated, and the central brain can direct them with considerable precision when an octopus opens a jar or squeezes through a gap. What the arms seem to have is a large degree of local autonomy, a capacity to handle the details of their own work without referring every decision upward.

That arrangement is worth thinking about precisely because it is so different from our own. We tend to picture intelligence as a single command center issuing orders to obedient limbs. The octopus suggests a different design, one in which a great deal of the thinking happens at the point of contact with the world, and in which the question of where the animal ends and everything else begins is answered, at least in part, by taste. It is a strange way to be an animal, and we are only beginning to understand it, but the octopus has been managing it for a very long time.

title: The Frog That Freezes
text:
In the forests of North America, a small brown frog spends much of the winter frozen. Not chilled, not sluggish, but frozen: if you were to find a wood frog under the leaf litter in January and pick it up, it would be hard to the touch, its eyes glazed white, its legs stiff. It would not be breathing. Its heart would not be beating. By every ordinary test it would be dead. And in the spring, when the ground thaws, it would thaw with it, and within a day or so it would be hopping off in search of a pond in which to breed.

Freezing is lethal to most animals for a simple physical reason. When water inside a cell turns to ice, the crystals grow and pierce the delicate membranes that hold the cell together, and when the ice melts, the cell falls apart. Even ice that forms outside the cells does damage, because as water freezes it leaves its dissolved salts behind in a shrinking pool of liquid, and that increasingly salty liquid draws water out of the cells, which shrink and collapse. An animal that freezes, in other words, faces two dangers at once: ice that tears and ice that dries.

The wood frog survives both, and the way it does so contains a surprise. The key substance is sugar. Soon after ice begins to form on the frog’s skin, its liver starts converting stored starch into glucose and pouring it into the blood at an extraordinary rate. Within hours, the level of sugar in the frog’s blood can rise to many times its normal value, a level that would be dangerous for a human. The glucose floods into the cells and acts as a kind of antifreeze, lowering the temperature at which their contents freeze and, just as important, keeping enough water inside them that they do not shrivel as ice grows around them. The surprise is the trigger. The frog does not begin preparing as the air grows cold. It begins when it actually starts to freeze.

What follows is a controlled freezing. Ice forms in the spaces between cells, in the body cavity, and under the skin, and by some measurements as much as two-thirds of the water in the frog’s body may end up as ice. The cells themselves, packed with sugar, stay liquid. The frog then waits, sometimes for weeks at a time, with no heartbeat and no breath, its tissues getting by on the small amount of energy they can make without oxygen. When the temperature rises, the frog is reported to thaw from the inside out, the reverse of what one might expect, and its heart starts beating again before its legs have fully thawed.

How far the strategy can be pushed turns out to depend on where the frog lives. Frogs from the milder parts of the range have been found to survive freezing only to a few degrees below zero Celsius. Some populations in Alaska, by contrast, have been reported to survive much colder temperatures, well below minus fifteen degrees, and to remain frozen for months on end. These northern frogs appear to build up larger stores of sugar and other protective compounds in the autumn, which suggests that the capacity to freeze is not a fixed trait of the species but something that has been tuned, population by population, to local winters.

It is easy to make too much of all this. The wood frog is not indestructible, and many frogs do not survive a hard winter. Freezing too fast, or too often, or for too long can kill it, and it depends on a blanket of leaves and snow to keep the temperature from dropping too far or too quickly. Its trick is a narrow one, fitted to particular conditions, and it would not work for most animals, including us.

Still, the frog has caught the attention of researchers who work on a very different problem. Human organs for transplant can be kept alive outside the body for only a matter of hours, and one of the great obstacles to storing them longer is that they cannot be frozen without being destroyed. The wood frog does every winter something that medicine cannot yet do at all. Nobody expects to freeze a kidney the way a frog freezes itself. But the frog is proof that the thing is possible in principle, and a hint that the answer, when it comes, may involve something as ordinary as sugar.

title: The Lake That Turns Over
text:
Twice a year, in spring and in autumn, many of the lakes of the temperate world turn over. Nothing visible happens. There is no churning at the surface and no sudden change in colour, and a swimmer might notice nothing at all. But over a few days or weeks, water from the bottom of the lake rises and water from the top sinks, and the whole body of water mixes from surface to floor. For the creatures living in it, this quiet overturning is one of the most important events of the year.

The reason it happens lies in an odd property of water. Most liquids grow steadily denser as they cool, so that the coldest liquid always sinks to the bottom. Water does this too, but only down to about four degrees Celsius. Below that temperature it begins to expand again, becoming slightly less dense as it approaches freezing, and when it finally turns to ice it expands further still, which is why ice floats. The densest water in a lake, therefore, is not the coldest water. It is water at about four degrees.

Consider what this means for a deep lake over a year. In summer, the sun warms the surface, and the warm water, being lighter, stays on top. Below it lies a layer of cold, dense water that the sun never reaches, and between the two is a narrow zone in which the temperature drops sharply. The layers resist mixing, and wind that ruffles the surface stirs only the top one. For months, the deep water is effectively sealed off from the air.

In autumn, the surface cools. As it approaches four degrees it grows denser than the water beneath it and sinks, and the wind, no longer opposed by a sharp difference in density, can drive the mixing all the way down. The lake turns over. Then, as winter comes and the surface cools past four degrees toward freezing, the order reverses: the coldest water now floats on top, ice forms at the surface, and the bottom settles at about four degrees, which is why fish can survive the winter in the depths of a lake whose surface is frozen solid. In spring the ice melts, the surface warms back through four degrees, and the lake turns over a second time.

The importance of all this becomes clear if you think about what the deep water lacks during its long isolation. Oxygen enters a lake at the surface, from the air and from plants that photosynthesize in the light. In summer, the sealed-off bottom layer receives none, while the dead plankton that sink into it are broken down by bacteria that use up what oxygen there is. By late summer the deepest water of a productive lake may be nearly without oxygen. The autumn turnover carries fresh oxygen down to the bottom and lifts nutrients that have collected there up toward the light, where they feed the next season’s growth. The lake, in effect, breathes twice a year.

Not every lake does. Some very deep lakes, and some whose bottom water is made unusually dense by dissolved salts or gases, never mix completely, and their deep water can remain isolated for years or even centuries. Usually this is merely a curiosity. Occasionally it is a danger. In 1986, Lake Nyos in Cameroon, whose deep water had accumulated large amounts of carbon dioxide seeping up from volcanic sources below, released a great cloud of the gas in a sudden overturn. The cloud, heavier than air, flowed down into the surrounding valleys and killed some seventeen hundred people. The exact trigger is still debated. Pipes have since been installed to vent the gas gradually.

Researchers have also begun to worry that the ordinary turnover of ordinary lakes may be changing. Warmer summers strengthen the layering and lengthen the season in which the bottom water is cut off, and milder winters mean that some lakes that once froze no longer do, and may mix differently as a result. The effects are still being worked out, and they will differ from lake to lake. But the odd behaviour of water near four degrees, which most people never think about, turns out to be the hinge on which the life of a lake swings.

title: Two Views on the Four-Day School Week
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by the superintendent of a rural school district. Passage B is adapted from an article by an education researcher. Both concern school districts that hold classes only four days a week.
text:
PASSAGE A

When our district moved to a four-day week six years ago, the letters to the local paper predicted disaster. Children would fall behind, parents would lose their jobs staying home to look after them, and the district would become the laughing stock of the county. I understand the alarm. I shared some of it. But the disaster did not come, and I have come to think that the change was the best decision our board has made in my time here.

The reason we did it was not the one people assume. Most outsiders think the four-day week is about saving money, and we did save some, on buses, heating, and substitute teachers, but the savings were smaller than the board had hoped. The real reason was hiring. We are a small district two hours from the nearest city, and for years we could not fill our open positions in mathematics and science. The first year we advertised a four-day week, we had more applicants for a single chemistry post than we had had for all of our science vacancies the year before. Teachers, it turns out, will drive a long way for a three-day weekend.

The school days are longer now, by a little over an hour, so that students spend nearly as many hours in class across the year as they did before. On Mondays the buildings stay open for students who need extra help, and our attendance has improved, partly because families schedule dental appointments and trips to the city on the day off instead of pulling children out of class. Teachers use part of the day off to plan lessons together, something they rarely had time to do before. Our test scores have not risen dramatically. They have not fallen, either.

I would not recommend the four-day week to every district. A city school with no trouble hiring has less to gain from it. But for a district like ours, the choice was never between four days and five days with a good teacher in every room. It was between four days with a teacher and five days without one.

PASSAGE B

The four-day school week has spread quietly through rural districts over the past two decades, and it has spread largely on the strength of stories like the ones districts tell about themselves: cheaper, happier, and no harm done. The stories are sincere. The trouble is that a district’s own test scores, taken alone, cannot tell us whether the schedule helped or hurt, because we do not know what would have happened to those scores with five days. A district whose scores stayed flat may have been headed for a rise; a district that saw a small dip may have been headed for a larger one, or for none at all.

When researchers have tried to answer that question by comparing districts that switched with similar districts that did not, the results have been mixed but not reassuring. Several studies have found small declines in achievement after a switch, especially in mathematics, and some have found larger declines in districts that did not lengthen their remaining days enough to make up the lost hours. A few found no effect. Almost none found gains. A small decline, repeated over the many years a child spends in school, is not a small thing.

The savings, meanwhile, are usually modest, often only a few percent of a district’s budget, because the largest cost, salaries, does not shrink when a building closes for a day. And the costs that are saved do not simply disappear; some of them are shifted onto families. A parent who works five days a week must find someone to look after a young child on the weekday the school is closed, and in a rural area the choices may be few and expensive. Some districts offer care on that day; many do not.

I do not doubt that the four-day week helps some districts hire teachers, and in places where the alternative is an empty classroom, that may well outweigh a small loss in test scores. But that is a trade-off, and it should be described as one. A district that tells parents the change costs nothing is not telling them the whole story.

title: Two Views on Bringing Back the Mammoth
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by a geneticist. Passage B is adapted from an essay by a conservation biologist. Both concern proposals to use genetic engineering to create animals resembling the extinct woolly mammoth.
text:
PASSAGE A

The last woolly mammoths are thought to have died on a remote island in the Arctic Ocean about four thousand years ago, long after their relatives on the mainland had vanished. For most of the time since, bringing them back has been the stuff of fiction. It is not quite fiction any longer. The mammoth’s closest living relative, the Asian elephant, shares the great majority of its genes, and tools now exist to edit the DNA of elephant cells, changing genes one at a time toward the versions found in mammoth remains: genes for a thick coat, for small ears that lose less heat, for a layer of insulating fat.

What came out of such a project would not be a mammoth in the strict sense. It would be an elephant with some of a mammoth’s traits, able, if things went well, to live in the cold. I think that is enough to justify the attempt. Some ecologists have argued that mammoths and other large grazers once kept the far north as open grassland, trampling shrubs and packing down snow in ways that may have helped keep the frozen ground beneath them from thawing. If that is right, a herd of cold-adapted elephants might one day help slow the thaw of permafrost that holds vast amounts of carbon. The idea is contested, and the evidence for it comes largely from small field experiments, but it is not fanciful.

I will concede that this is a long way off, and that it may not work. But the techniques developed along the way would be valuable in themselves. Methods for editing and growing the cells of a large, slow-breeding mammal could help endangered species whose populations have grown so small that they have lost much of their genetic diversity, including, perhaps, the Asian elephant itself. Even a project that never produces a single mammoth-like calf might pay for itself in what it teaches. Science has often reached its most useful results while aiming at something else.

PASSAGE B

I understand the appeal of the mammoth. Few images are more likely to capture the public imagination than a shaggy giant walking out of the ice age into the present. But I have spent my career trying to keep living species from disappearing, and when I look at proposals to recreate extinct ones, I mostly see what they would cost the animals we still have.

Consider the elephant. An Asian elephant carries a calf for nearly two years, and the species is itself endangered. Any serious attempt to produce a mammoth-like animal would require either many pregnancies in elephants or an artificial womb that does not yet exist, and it is hard to see how the first could be justified for an endangered species that reproduces so slowly. The calf, if one were born, would be a highly social animal with no herd of its own kind to learn from. Elephants learn a great deal from their elders. It is not obvious what a mammoth-like calf would learn, or from whom. Raising such an animal alone, or among elephants whose ancestors evolved for the tropics, would be an experiment on a creature that could not consent to it and might well suffer from it.

There is a subtler risk as well. If the public comes to believe that extinction can be reversed, the urgency of preventing it may fade. Why spend money protecting a habitat today if a species can be rebuilt from its DNA tomorrow? No scientist involved in these projects has made that argument, but an argument does not need to be made aloud to have its effect.

I do not dismiss the science. Some of the tools being developed may yet prove useful to conservation, and I would welcome them. But they should be developed for the species that are still here, which can be saved at a fraction of the price, and whose last members are not frozen in the ground but alive, and running out of time. Every dollar spent on a mammoth is a dollar not spent on rhinos, on elephants, or on the many less glamorous species that are slipping away, some of them before anyone has studied them at all.

title: The Graft
text:
I had been told the orchard would be good for me, which is what adults say about anything they have already decided. My mother drove me up on the first Saturday in April, left a bag of groceries and a typed list of my allergies on my grandfather’s kitchen table, and was back on the highway before the kettle boiled. My grandfather read the list twice, looked at me over his glasses, and said that as far as he knew nobody had ever been allergic to apples. I told him I was allergic to being fifteen and stranded three hours from anyone I knew. He said that one usually cleared up on its own.

The orchard was smaller than I remembered and a good deal uglier. Half the trees were old Baldwins that my grandmother had loved and nobody else wanted; the fruit was hard and sour and kept all winter in the cellar, which had mattered once and did not matter now. The rest were a mix he could not name, planted by the previous owner, and several of them were dead in a way that even I could recognize. He did not seem troubled by any of it. He walked the rows each morning with a pocketknife and a roll of green tape, stopping at certain trees the way other men stop at a fence to talk to a neighbor.

On the third day he handed me the knife. He had a bundle of cuttings wrapped in damp newspaper, pencil-thin sticks he had taken in February from a tree two farms over, and he wanted them set into the branches of the Baldwins. Grafting, he called it, as though the word explained itself. You cut the old branch clean, split the stub, and wedge the new stick into the split so that the thin green layer under the bark of each lines up with the other. If the layers touch, the two will grow together into one limb. If they miss by the width of a hair, he said, you have made a very expensive piece of kindling.

I missed a great deal. My cuts were ragged and my wedges sat crooked, and by lunchtime the only thing I had grafted successfully was a strip of tape to my own thumb. My grandfather did not correct me so much as stand beside me, doing the same thing more slowly, until I found I was copying the angle of his wrist without meaning to. He talked the whole time, though not about grafting. He talked about the neighbor whose tree the cuttings came from, a woman named Ruth who had taught at the county school with my grandmother for thirty years and who, he said, had never once been on time for anything, including her own wedding.

It was not until the end of the week that I asked why he was bothering. The Baldwins were old, the new wood would take three or four years to bear, and he was, I pointed out with all the tact of a fifteen-year-old, not getting any younger. He considered this seriously, the way he considered everything I said, which I found more irritating than being ignored. Then he told me that the tree two farms over was one my grandmother had planted in Ruth’s yard the year Ruth retired, grown from a cutting of her own favorite tree, which had blown down in a storm before I was born. Ruth was selling the farm in the fall.

“So they’re Grandma’s apples,” I said. “Coming back.” He said that was one way to put it. Another way, he said, was that the Baldwins would do the rooting and the new wood would do the fruiting, and neither one was much use without the other. He said it lightly, and went back to his tape, and I understood that I was not expected to answer.

I went home at the end of April with a sunburn and a small white scar on my thumb that I still have. The next spring I asked to go back, and told my mother it was because the city bored me. Of the forty grafts we set that week, thirty-one took. My grandfather knew exactly which of the nine failures were mine. He was kind enough never to count them out loud, though I have always suspected he kept a list.

title: Do Not Duplicate
text:
For twenty-two years I have cut keys in a booth at the far end of the Eastgate mall, between a shoe-repair counter and a stand that sells pretzels, and in that time I have learned that people will tell a key cutter things they would not tell a priest. They do not mean to. They put a key on my counter and wait while the machine whines, and the silence makes them nervous, and out it comes: the divorce, the new job, the roommate who cannot be trusted with the good cereal. I nod. I have found that a nod is most of what anyone wants.

The key the young woman put on my counter that Tuesday was an ordinary brass house key, worn smooth at the head, with DO NOT DUPLICATE stamped along the blade in letters somebody had paid extra for. People think those words are a law. In most places, as far as I have ever been able to find out, they are closer to a polite request, and a machine does not read. But I have my own rule, which is that when a key tells me not to copy it, I ask why before I do.

She had the answer ready, which is usually a bad sign. It was her mother’s apartment, she said. Her mother was eighty-one and had started leaving the stove on, and the building manager would not give out a spare without the tenant’s signature, and her mother would not sign because she did not think anything was wrong. The young woman said all this very fast, looking at the pretzel stand instead of at me. Then she said, more slowly, that she was not trying to take anything from anybody. She just wanted to be able to get in.

I have heard a great many stories across that counter, and most of them are true, and some of the true ones are the ones I should have refused. I did not know which kind this was. I thought about the old woman, whom I would never meet, and what she might say about a stranger in a mall copying her front door. I thought about the stove. In the end I cut it, because I could not see how a daughter with a key was more dangerous than a burner with nobody watching it, and I charged her the usual four dollars and told her to go carefully.

That night I told my wife about it over dinner, and she asked me the question I had not asked the young woman, which was whether her mother knew. I said I supposed not. My wife said that in that case I had not copied a key so much as taken a side, and that I should at least be honest with myself about which side it was. She was right, as she usually is when she has had a whole afternoon to think and I have had four minutes. I slept badly, and told myself that I would never know how it turned out, which is the ordinary condition of my trade.

For a week nothing happened. Then on the following Tuesday an old woman in a green raincoat came down the long corridor from the parking garage, slowly, holding the handrail, and put a brass house key on my counter with DO NOT DUPLICATE stamped along the blade. She wanted a copy, she said. It was for her daughter. Her daughter worried too much, and she had decided it would be easier on both of them if the girl simply had one.

I am sixty-three years old and I have been in the key business since before that daughter was born, and I stood there holding that key as if I had never seen one. I could have told her. I thought about it for as long as it takes the machine to warm up, which is not long. Then I cut the key, and charged her four dollars, and wished her a good afternoon, and she went back up the corridor holding the rail.

I have wondered since whether I did right. The daughter now has two keys to one door, and neither woman knows the other has been to see me. The mother believes she gave the key freely; the daughter believes she took it. It seems to me there are worse arrangements. A key is only a small piece of metal cut to the shape of somebody’s trust, and I have never yet been asked to cut one that fit exactly.

title: The Last Forecast
text:
Every morning at five-fifteen, Maren Holt sat down in a room the size of a closet above the hardware store in Port Anselm and read the marine forecast into a microphone that had been old when she was hired. Wind southwest ten to fifteen knots, backing south in the afternoon. Seas three to five feet. Visibility good, reducing in patchy fog. She had read some version of those sentences perhaps six thousand times, and she had long since stopped believing that anyone heard them.

She had reasons for this belief, and she was prepared to list them. The fishing fleet the forecast had been started for had shrunk from forty boats to nine. Every one of the nine carried a telephone that could show the wind at the harbor mouth, updated every few minutes, in colors. The station’s own survey, taken two years earlier, had found that its morning audience was too small to measure, a phrase the station manager had repeated at a staff meeting as though it were a joke, and which Maren privately thought was the most accurate description of her career anyone had yet produced.

She had not always been so dismissive. When she started, at twenty-four, she had rehearsed the names of the headlands and shoals in the car on the way to work, and she had written to the weather office to ask what backing meant, and had been pleased to learn that it meant the wind was turning counterclockwise. Somewhere in the years since, the forecast had become a thing her mouth did while her mind made lists. She could not have said when it happened. That, she supposed, was the nature of it.

So when the manager told her in March that the forecast would be dropped at the end of the month and replaced with an extra half hour of recorded music, she was surprised to find that she minded. She did not say so. She said that it made sense, which it did, and that she could use the sleep, which was also true. Then she went home and lay awake until four, and at five-fifteen she read the forecast with more care than she had given it in years, as if someone might be grading her.

Somebody was. On the third morning of her last week, halfway through the outlook for the outer waters, the studio telephone rang, which it had not done at that hour in living memory. The voice on the other end belonged to a man named Gus Aberline, who fished alone out of the north harbor, and he wanted her to know that she had been pronouncing Cape Tessaly wrong for as long as he had been listening, which was nineteen years. It was TESS-a-lee, not tess-AY-lee. He had not wanted to say anything before. He was saying so now because he had heard the forecast was ending, and he thought she ought to have it right for the last few days.

Maren asked him, because she could not help it, why he listened at all when he had the telephone with the colors. Gus said the telephone told him what the wind was doing. The forecast told him what somebody who knew the coast thought it was going to do, and those were not the same thing. Besides, he said, it was company. He had left the harbor in the dark every morning for thirty years, and for most of them hers had been the first voice he heard.

After that the telephone rang more often. A woman who ran a guesthouse on the point called to say that she timed her bread by the forecast. Two more of the nine boats called. A retired harbor pilot called to complain, at length, about the phrase patchy fog, which he considered unscientific. None of this changed the manager’s mind, and Maren had not expected it to. Nine boats were nine boats.

On the last morning she read the forecast slowly and said Cape Tessaly the way Gus had taught her. When she finished she did not say goodbye, because the forecast had never said goodbye, and she was not going to let it start now. She switched off the microphone and sat for a moment in the small warm room, and heard the first of the recorded music begin on the monitor, bright and a little too loud, as if nothing had happened.

title: What a Free Space Costs
text:
Few things in a city feel as much like a natural right as a free place to park. Drivers who would never expect a free sandwich expect a free curb, and a city council that proposes charging for one can count on a crowded meeting. Yet the free space is not free. Someone pays for the land it occupies, the asphalt that covers it, and the officers who enforce its time limits, and a growing number of planners argue that the way we pay for it makes cities worse for almost everyone, including the drivers who defend it most fiercely.

The argument begins with a simple observation. When something valuable is given away, people line up for it, and on a busy street the line takes the form of cars circling the block. Drivers hunting for an open space add traffic that would not otherwise exist, burn fuel, and slow the buses and delivery vans around them. How much traffic this cruising accounts for is disputed. One widely repeated estimate put it at around a third of the cars in some busy districts, but later studies in other cities have found much smaller shares, and the true figure almost certainly varies from street to street. Even the lower estimates, though, describe a real cost that no one is charged for.

Planners who make this case usually propose the same remedy: price curb parking so that, on each block, one or two spaces stay open at most times of day. The price is not meant to raise money but to keep a space available, and so it rises where spaces are scarce and falls where they are plentiful. San Francisco tried a version of this approach in the early 2010s, adjusting meter prices block by block every few months according to how full each block had been. Evaluations reported that finding a space became easier, although, as critics pointed out, other changes in the city at the time make the program’s exact effect difficult to isolate.

The second half of the argument concerns parking that drivers never see being paid for. For decades many cities required new buildings to include a minimum number of off-street spaces, often according to formulas whose origins nobody could trace. A single space in a parking garage can cost tens of thousands of dollars to build, and that cost does not disappear. It is folded into rents, into the price of groceries, into the budget of a small restaurant that must provide spaces before it is allowed to open. People who do not own a car pay it too.

In recent years a number of cities have begun to drop these requirements, and the early results are instructive, if not conclusive. Where minimums have been lifted, developers have not stopped building parking; they have built less of it, and on some sites near frequent transit, where their tenants did not want it, none. A few of the buildings that resulted could not have been built at all under the old rules, because the lot was too small to hold both the apartments and the garage the formula demanded. Whether the lower rents that advocates predicted will follow is harder to say, and will take years to measure.

None of this means that pricing parking is painless, and its advocates sometimes write as if it were. A nurse who works the night shift in a neighborhood with poor bus service did not choose to drive because she underestimated the social cost of curb space. A small shop on a street where meters suddenly appear may lose customers to a mall with an enormous free lot. Any honest proposal has to reckon with people like these, whether by spending meter revenue on the street where it was collected, by exempting some workers, or simply by moving slowly.

Still, the alternative to priced parking is not a world in which parking costs nothing. It is a world in which the cost is hidden and spread across everyone, including the people who use it least. A free space works the way a free lunch does in the old saying: someone has paid for it, and the only question is whether the people enjoying it know who. Pricing it openly would not so much make parking more expensive as make its cost visible to the people who use it.

title: The Library of Things
text:
Somewhere in almost every discussion of sharing, a statistic appears about the power drill. The average drill, the claim goes, is used for a total of thirteen minutes in its entire life. The number has been repeated in business books, in lectures, and in at least one advertisement for a sharing app, and as far as anyone has been able to tell, it has no source at all. Nobody seems to have measured it. It survives because it feels true: most of us own things we almost never use, and the drill in the garage is the obvious example.

The libraries of things that have opened in a number of cities over the past two decades are built on that feeling. A library of things lends objects rather than books: drills and ladders, but also tents, sewing machines, pasta makers, carpet cleaners, and, in one library I visited, a full-size inflatable snowman. Members pay a small fee or none at all, borrow what they need for a week, and bring it back. The idea is not new. Tool lending libraries existed in some American cities by the 1970s, and a few of those are still open. Most are run by volunteers, and many operate out of a single room in a public library or community center. What is new is the scale of the claims made for them.

Those claims are usually environmental. If twenty households share one drill instead of buying twenty, the reasoning goes, nineteen drills are never manufactured, shipped, or thrown away. On paper the arithmetic is irresistible. In practice it depends on things that are much harder to count. A borrower who would otherwise have bought a drill saves one; a borrower who would have used a neighbor’s, or done without, saves nothing, and may have driven across town twice to pick it up and return it.

There is a second difficulty, which the libraries themselves are often candid about. Tools that are shared wear out faster than tools that are not. A drill owned by one careful person may last twenty years; the same drill lent to forty strangers, some of whom have never held one, may last two. Several coordinators told me that their most expensive problem was not theft, which was rare, but repair, and that the cheapest tools were often a false economy because they broke on their third or fourth loan. A library that replaces its drills every few years is still saving something, but less than the arithmetic on the brochure suggests.

The volunteers who run these libraries are, in my experience, more modest than their brochures. When I asked the coordinator of one small library what it was for, she did not mention drills or carbon at all. She said that most of her members were renters in small apartments with no room to store a ladder they needed twice a year. Others were trying out a hobby before committing to it: a person who borrows a sewing machine for a month and discovers she hates sewing has avoided buying a machine that would have sat in a closet for a decade.

She also told me something I did not expect. The busiest hour of the week was Saturday morning, and on most Saturdays at least half the people who came in did not borrow anything. They came to ask how to fix something. The library held a repair session in its back room, and members who knew how to rewire a lamp or sharpen a blade taught members who did not. The objects on the shelves, she suggested, were partly an excuse. What the library really lent was knowledge, and a reason to be in a room with people who had it.

It would be easy to take all this as a reason to dismiss the environmental case, and I do not think that would be right. Some borrowing surely does replace buying, and a library that lends a few hundred tools a year probably keeps some of them out of landfills. But the thirteen-minute drill tells us more about what we want to believe than about what these places do. The strongest argument for a library of things may be the one its brochures rarely make: that it teaches people to take care of what they already own.

title: Who the Census Misses
text:
Every ten years, the United States tries to count everyone living in it, and every ten years it falls short in ways that are, by now, fairly predictable. The people the census is most likely to miss are the ones you might expect: renters who move often, residents of remote rural areas, people who distrust the government, people living in housing that does not look like housing from the street. The group that has been missed at the highest rate in recent counts, however, is one that surprises almost everyone who hears about it. It is not the elderly, or the homeless, or recent immigrants. It is babies.

Children under five have been undercounted in census after census for decades, and by some measures the problem has grown worse rather than better. Estimates published after the 2020 count suggested that roughly one young child in twenty had been missed, a rate higher than that of any adult group. This is strange on its face. A baby cannot move out, does not distrust the government, and in most cases lives with at least one adult who was counted. How is it possible to count a mother and miss the child she is holding?

It is fair to ask how anyone knows. For young children, the answer is unusually clean. Births in the United States are recorded almost without exception, and deaths among small children, though tragic, are few enough to be tracked closely. By starting from the birth records of the previous five years and adjusting for deaths and migration, demographers can estimate how many children under five ought to exist with more confidence than they can for any adult age group. When the census returns a smaller number, the gap is hard to explain away.

Researchers who have studied the question point first to how households are arranged. Young children are especially likely to live in complicated situations: with a grandparent while a parent works elsewhere, with a parent who divides time between two homes, in apartments shared by more than one family. The census form asks the person filling it out to list everyone who usually lives at the address, and in a crowded or shifting household the answer can be genuinely unclear. A grandmother may assume that the child’s mother listed him at her own apartment; the mother may assume that the grandmother did. Between two careful adults, each certain the other has it covered, a child can slip through the floor.

A second explanation is simpler and a little uncomfortable. Some adults, asked to list everyone living in a household, do not think of an infant as a member of it in quite the same way. Follow-up interviews have turned up respondents who left a baby off the form and, when asked why, said they thought the form was about the people who lived there, or did not realize newborns were meant to be included. Nobody meant to hide anyone. The error is not a lie. It is a question read more narrowly than it was written.

Why should any of this matter? Because the count is not simply a curiosity. Census figures are used to divide seats in Congress among the states and to distribute federal money for programs such as school funding and children’s health care. A community whose young children are undercounted may receive less than its share for a decade afterward, and it will be short precisely for the services those children are about to need. The census is taken once, and its numbers are used for all ten years that follow.

It is tempting to conclude that the census should simply try harder, and to some extent that is right. Outreach through hospitals, day-care centers, and pediatricians’ offices has been proposed and, in places, tried. Some researchers have suggested rewording the form to name babies and young children explicitly, on the theory that people answer the question they are actually asked. But the history of the problem suggests caution. The undercount of young children has survived decades of effort, several redesigns of the questionnaire, and the move to answering online, which suggests that its causes lie less in how hard the government counts than in how families understand the question. A form can ask about everyone who lives in a home. It cannot make every household agree on who that is.

title: The Hermit in the Garden
text:
Walk far enough through certain English landscape gardens and you will come upon a ruin that was never anything else. It may be a Gothic arch standing alone in a meadow, a broken tower on a hill, or a crumbling temple beside a lake, and at a distance it will look like the remains of some grand building that time has worn away. It is nothing of the kind. It was built, in most cases in the eighteenth century, to look ruined from the day it was finished. The owners of these estates paid architects to design decay.

The fashion puzzles modern visitors, and it is worth taking seriously rather than laughing at. The landscape garden of that era was meant to be walked through like a series of paintings, and its designers borrowed from painters of the previous century who had placed classical ruins in their imagined countrysides. A ruin gave a view a mood. It suggested the passage of time, the fall of empires, the smallness of any single life, and it did so while the visitor strolled toward the tea house. Some estates placed their ruins so that they would be seen from a particular bench or window, and laid out paths that revealed them only at the last turn. The pleasure lay in feeling a large, sad thought at no personal risk.

Some owners went further. At a handful of estates, according to accounts that historians still debate, a landowner built a rustic hermitage in the woods and advertised for a hermit to live in it. The terms reported in some of these stories are remarkable: the hermit was to let his hair and nails grow, wear a coarse robe, speak to no one, and remain on the property for years in exchange for a sum paid at the end. How many such hermits actually existed, and how long any of them lasted, is unclear. At least one, it is said, was dismissed after being found in the local tavern.

It is easy to see all this as the height of aristocratic silliness, and in part it was. A man who pays another man to sit in a damp hut and look thoughtful has confused wisdom with its costume. Yet the sham ruin and the hired hermit were answering something real. The eighteenth century was a period of rapid change in England, of new roads and enclosed fields and sudden fortunes, and the garden ruin allowed the people who were building that new world to imagine it already old and gently fallen. Some of the same families who commissioned ruins were busy pulling down genuinely old buildings to make room for new ones.

There is a lesson here, I think, about how we like our past. The ruins in these gardens were never allowed to decay much further than their builders intended. Gardeners kept the ivy trimmed to a picturesque amount; stones that fell were sometimes put back. The ruin was fixed at the precise moment of melancholy its owner had paid for. A real ruin, by contrast, keeps falling down. It is inconvenient and dangerous, and eventually it is simply gone.

Several of the best-known sham ruins have outlasted the families who paid for them, and some are now protected as historic buildings in their own right, which produces some strange arguments. A conservator asked to preserve a fake ruin must decide what, exactly, she is preserving: the building as it was put up, already broken, or the building as it has since been genuinely weathered by two and a half centuries of English rain. The false decay has acquired real decay on top of it, and it is not always possible to tell the two apart.

We have not stopped building sham ruins, although we no longer call them that. The new restaurant with brick distressed to look a century old, the shopping street designed to resemble a village that never existed, the jeans sold already torn: each offers the feeling of age without its costs. I do not say this to scold anyone. I have bought the jeans. But the eighteenth-century garden is a reminder that nostalgia has always been something people were willing to manufacture, and that what they wanted from the past was usually a mood, not the past itself.

title: The Indexer’s Art
text:
Nobody reads an index. People consult it, which is different, and they consult it in a particular mood: impatient, a little suspicious, wanting one fact and wanting it now. I have been writing indexes for other people’s books for nearly twenty years, and I have come to think of my readers as the least patient people in the world. They will never thank me. If I have done my job, they will not notice that I exist. If I have not, they will blame the author.

The index at the back of a book looks like the simplest thing in it, an alphabetical list of words with numbers beside them, and that appearance is the source of most misunderstandings about my work. An index is not a list of the words in a book. A computer can produce that list in a second, and the result, which is called a concordance, is useful to scholars of Shakespeare and nearly useless to anyone else. A concordance of a biography will tell you every page on which the word mother appears. It will not tell you on which pages the subject’s mother is actually discussed, and it will say nothing at all about the chapter in which she is never named but is the subject of every paragraph.

That chapter is where an indexer earns her fee. The work is closer to reading than to typing. I read the whole book, usually twice, and ask of each passage not what words it uses but what it is about, and then what a reader who wanted that subject would look up. Readers do not look up the author’s vocabulary; they look up their own. A book on gardening may speak throughout of soil amendment, but someone who wants to know what to do with coffee grounds will look under compost, and a good index has to be waiting there with a cross-reference.

The decisions multiply quickly. Should an entry be filed under the person, with the event beneath it, or under the event, with the person beneath it? There is no rule that settles such questions; there is only the reader to imagine. Both, perhaps, but an index that lists everything twice doubles in length and becomes harder to use. How finely should a large subject be divided? An entry followed by forty undivided page numbers, which indexers call a string, is a small act of cruelty, since it forces the reader to check forty pages. Divide the same entry into twenty subheadings, though, and the reader must now read a paragraph of index to find a page of book.

I should be fair to the machines, which are improving. Software now handles much of the drudgery that used to take up half of my time: sorting entries, updating page numbers after a book has been reset, catching an entry that points to a page where its subject no longer appears. Some publishers have begun to experiment with indexes generated almost entirely by programs that try to guess what a passage is about, and a few of the results I have seen are better than I expected. For a reference book with a rigid structure, in which every topic has its own clearly labeled section, such a program may do perfectly well.

For most books, though, the hardest part of indexing is not finding the subjects but judging them. An indexer has to decide that a passing mention is trivial and that a page without the keyword is essential, and those decisions depend on understanding what the author was trying to do. That is the part of the work that most resembles criticism, and it is the part I would be least willing to hand over. A poor index is not merely inconvenient. It quietly misrepresents a book, promising subjects it barely covers and hiding the ones it cares about most.

Once, years ago, a historian whose book I had indexed wrote to tell me that she had learned something from my work. Reading the index, she had discovered that she had written far more about the price of grain than she had realized. She seemed a little alarmed. I took it as the highest compliment I have ever received, though I am not certain she meant it as one. Every book has a secret subject, I sometimes think, and the index is where it shows.

title: The Porch and the Street
text:
For much of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, a great many American houses were built with a deep front porch, and on warm evenings a great many Americans sat on them. The porch was not quite indoors and not quite out. It belonged to the family, but it faced the street, and anyone walking past could be greeted, called over, or pointedly ignored. Historians of domestic life have described it as a kind of social valve, a place where a household could open itself to the neighborhood by degrees and close again when it chose.

The porch also did practical work. Before electric fans, a shaded porch was often the coolest place a family had on a summer evening, and in many towns it was where courting couples sat within sight of a watchful parent, where news was traded, and where children were kept in view while they played in the street. It was, in other words, not a decoration but a room, and a heavily used one. Anyone who grew up with one can usually say which chair was whose.

By the middle of the twentieth century the porch was in retreat, and the usual explanation names three culprits. Air conditioning made the inside of a house more comfortable than the outside on a summer night. Television gave families a reason to stay in the living room after dark. And the automobile turned the street in front of the house from a place where people walked into a place where cars passed, noisy and fast and full of strangers who could not be greeted. New houses were built with the garage in front and a patio or deck behind, where the family could be outdoors without being seen.

I find this account persuasive as far as it goes, and I have no wish to acquit any of its three villains. But it tends to treat the porch as a casualty, something taken from people against their will, and I am not sure that is right. The backyard deck was not forced on anyone. It was chosen, and chosen enthusiastically, by families who had spent their childhoods on porches and knew exactly what they were giving up. Privacy, it turned out, was something many of them wanted more than they had been able to say. The porch had made a household available to its neighbors whether it wished to be or not.

In recent decades the porch has returned, at least in appearance. Developers of new neighborhoods, some of them designed to feel like the small towns of a century ago, have put porches back on the fronts of houses, sometimes as a requirement written into the neighborhood’s rules. Critics have pointed out that many of these porches are too shallow to hold a chair, perhaps four feet deep, suitable for standing at the front door with a package and not much else. They signal a porch without providing one. It would be easy to mock them, and some writers have.

I am less inclined to. A shallow porch is a statement about what the owners want their house to seem like, and what they want it to seem like is open, friendly, and connected to the street. That is not nothing. Buildings shape behavior, but they also record wishes, and the return of the decorative porch records a wish that its owners may not yet be ready to act on. A family that sits on its deck in the evening and keeps a porch on the front of the house is telling us that it values privacy and misses company, both at once, which is an honest description of most people I know.

Whether the deep porch will come back is a harder question. Air conditioning is not going anywhere, and neither is the car. But in some older neighborhoods I have noticed a change. Where streets have been narrowed, traffic slowed, and sidewalks widened, the porches that survived from an earlier era are being used again, with chairs and potted plants and, on warm evenings, people. The lesson may be that the porch was never really about the house. It was about the street, and it will return when the street gives people a reason to face it. Porches follow sidewalks, not the other way around.

title: The Mold That Drew a Railway
text:
Physarum polycephalum does not look like much. In the wild it lives on rotting logs and damp leaves in shaded forests, where it appears as a bright yellow smear, sometimes as large as a dinner plate, spreading in a network of branching veins. It is neither a plant nor an animal, and although it was long classified as a fungus, it is not one of those either. For much of its life it is a single enormous cell containing many thousands of nuclei, which creeps across its surroundings at a rate of perhaps a few centimeters an hour, engulfing bacteria and spores as it goes. It has no brain and no nervous system of any kind.

It is therefore a little embarrassing, for creatures that do have brains, how well it solves certain problems. In a now well-known experiment published in 2000, a team of Japanese researchers let a slime mold fill a small plastic maze and then placed pieces of food, oat flakes, at the entrance and the exit. Over the next several hours the mold withdrew from the dead ends and the longer routes and gathered itself into a single thick tube connecting the two food sources along one of the shortest available paths. The researchers were careful to say that the mold was not thinking. What it was doing, however, looked from the outside very much like a solution.

The explanation lies in how the organism moves material through its own body. The veins of a slime mold pulse rhythmically, pushing fluid back and forth, and tubes that carry more flow tend to thicken while tubes that carry less tend to wither. Where food is found, flow increases. The result is a kind of feedback: successful routes grow stronger and unsuccessful ones fade, with no part of the organism needing to know the layout of the maze as a whole. The solution emerges from a great many local adjustments, each of which is simple.

The same principle helps explain what happens when food is placed at several points instead of two. The mold does not simply find the shortest route between each pair. It builds a network that balances competing demands, keeping the total length of its tubes fairly short while also adding a few redundant links, so that if one tube is cut, nutrients can still reach the rest of the cell by another path. That balance is exactly the one human engineers try to strike when they design networks of roads, pipes, or cables.

A decade later, some of the same researchers tried something more ambitious. They arranged oat flakes on a wet surface in the positions of cities around Tokyo, placed the mold at the location of Tokyo itself, and used patches of light, which the mold avoids, to stand in for mountains and coastline. Within about a day the mold had connected the flakes with a network of tubes. When the researchers compared this network with the region’s actual railway system, they found the two strikingly similar in how efficiently they linked the cities, how much total track they required, and how well they could survive a break in any one link.

It is easy to overstate what this means, and headlines did. The mold did not design a railway, and the engineers who built Tokyo’s lines had to consider land prices, politics, and existing towns, none of which the mold was asked to handle. The comparison showed something narrower and perhaps more interesting: that a simple rule of reinforcing what works, applied everywhere at once, can arrive at networks resembling those that human planners reach by deliberate effort over decades. Some engineers have since studied the mold’s rule as a possible model for designing networks of their own.

The most surprising finding may concern memory. Later experiments suggested that a slime mold avoids ground covered by the trail of slime it has already left behind, so that when it is searching for food it tends not to cover the same ground twice. If that interpretation is right, the organism stores a record of where it has been not inside itself but on the surface it has crossed. Researchers have described this, cautiously, as a form of external memory. A creature with no brain, it seems, may keep part of its mind on the floor.

title: One Tree, Forty Thousand Trunks
text:
In the mountains of south-central Utah, on the slopes above a small lake, there is a grove of quaking aspen that looks, to a hiker passing through it, like any other stand of aspen: tall white trunks marked with black scars, leaves that tremble in the slightest wind and turn gold in autumn. The hiker would have no way of knowing that the grove is, by several reasonable definitions, a single tree. Its tens of thousands of trunks share one root system and one set of genes. Researchers call it Pando, from a Latin word meaning “I spread.”

Aspen can reproduce from seed, but in much of the American West they more often reproduce by sending up new shoots from their roots. Each shoot grows into what looks like an independent tree, but it remains connected underground to its parent and to its siblings, and it is genetically identical to them. Over centuries a single seedling can give rise to a whole stand of such stems, a colony that botanists call a clone. Most aspen clones cover an acre or two. Pando covers something over a hundred acres and has been estimated to include more than forty thousand stems, which is why it is often described as one of the heaviest living organisms known.

The comparison to a single tree is not merely a figure of speech. Because the stems share roots, they can share resources: water and sugars gathered in one part of the clone can travel underground to another, and a young shoot coming up in the shade of older trunks may be fed for a time by the root system it grew from. When fire or disease kills the trunks above ground, the roots often survive and send up new shoots, sometimes in great numbers. For an aspen clone, losing every visible tree can be less a death than a haircut.

For a time the claim that Pando was one organism rested largely on appearance.
