Every trunk in it leafs out on the same day in spring and turns color at the same time in autumn, on a schedule that differs from those of neighboring clones, so that on the right October afternoon the edge of the colony can be seen from a distance as a line between gold and green. Genetic testing later confirmed what the leaves had suggested. Samples taken from across the grove shared the same genetic signature, one distinct from that of the aspen around it.

How old Pando is remains uncertain, and the question is harder than it sounds. The trunks themselves are young; an individual aspen stem rarely lives much more than a century or so. What is old is the root system and the genetic line, and neither can be dated by counting rings. Estimates have ranged from several thousand years to far more, and one recent study, which tried to date the clone by counting small genetic changes that had built up in different parts of it, suggested an age greater than most earlier estimates had allowed, though its authors acknowledged wide uncertainty.

What is not in doubt is that Pando is in trouble. A healthy clone constantly replaces its old trunks with new ones, and in much of Pando that replacement has stalled. Young shoots come up as they always have, but deer and elk, whose numbers in the area have been high, eat them before they can grow out of reach. Surveys of the grove have reported sections in which almost no stems younger than several decades remain. The result is a forest of old trees with almost no young ones among them, a grove that looks full and is quietly aging toward collapse.

Here the story takes a hopeful turn, because the problem has proved fixable wherever anyone has tried. When sections of the grove were fenced to keep browsing animals out, young stems sprang up inside the fences in large numbers, and within a few years those sections looked like a different forest. Fencing has its own difficulties: fences break, animals find gaps, and enclosing an entire hundred-acre clone is expensive. But the experiment showed that the root system beneath the grove is still vigorous. It has been sending up shoots all along. The grove, it turns out, has not been failing to grow. It has been failing to be allowed to.

title: The Moon Is Leaving
text:
On several of the missions that landed on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, astronauts set up a device that looks, in photographs, like a small tray of glass marbles set into an aluminum frame. It is an array of reflectors, each shaped like the corner of a cube, and it has the useful property of sending light back exactly the way it came. Observatories on Earth have been firing laser pulses at these arrays ever since and timing how long the light takes to return. The round trip takes about two and a half seconds, and by measuring it precisely, scientists can now track the distance to the Moon to within a few millimeters. Other reflectors of the same kind were carried to the Moon by uncrewed Soviet rovers.

The best-known result of these measurements is that the Moon is moving away from us. It is doing so slowly, at a rate of roughly three point eight centimeters a year, about as fast as a fingernail grows. The cause is the same force that raises the tides. The Moon’s gravity stretches the Earth’s oceans into a pair of bulges, but because the Earth spins faster than the Moon orbits, the planet’s rotation drags those bulges slightly ahead of the line between the two bodies. The bulge nearer the Moon then pulls on it, very gently, in the direction of its travel, and that small forward tug slowly lifts the Moon into a wider orbit.

The same exchange has a cost on this end. The friction of the tides acts as a brake on the Earth’s spin, and so the day is growing longer, by something on the order of two thousandths of a second per century. That is far too little for anyone to notice in a lifetime. Over geological time, though, it adds up, and there is evidence of it written in stone. Some fossil corals laid down growth bands that appear to record both days and years, and in corals roughly four hundred million years old, researchers have counted around four hundred daily bands to a yearly cycle. If that reading is right, the year then held about four hundred shorter days.

Here the story contains a surprise. If the Moon had always receded at its present rate, then running the clock backward would bring it very close to the Earth only about one and a half billion years ago, which is far too recent. The Moon is thought to be well over four billion years old, and the geological record shows no sign of the catastrophe that so close an approach would have caused. Either the Moon formed far more recently than the evidence says, which almost no one believes, or something about the present moment is unusual. The present rate, in other words, must be unusually fast.

The leading explanation involves the shape of the oceans. How strongly the tides brake the Earth depends on how the water in each ocean basin sloshes in response to the Moon’s pull, and that depends on the size and arrangement of the basins, which change as the continents drift. At present, some researchers argue, the Atlantic in particular is close to a size at which its natural sloshing matches the rhythm of the tides, so that the tides there are amplified, the way a child on a swing goes higher when pushed at just the right moment. In other eras, with the continents arranged differently, the tides were weaker and the Moon retreated more slowly. Computer models of ancient oceans, reconstructed from the past positions of the continents, appear to support this idea, though they carry large uncertainties of their own.

None of this should cause anyone alarm. The Moon will not escape, and long before its retreat could matter in any practical way, other changes in the Sun and the Earth will have made the question moot. But the measurement has a quiet grandeur. With a laser, a telescope, and a few trays of glass left behind half a century ago, it is possible to watch the Moon edge away from us by a few centimeters each year, and to find, in that small number, a record of drifting continents and the changing shape of the sea. An experiment begun to test theories of gravity has turned out to be a way of reading the history of the oceans.

title: Two Views on the Phone-Free School
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by a high school principal. Passage B is adapted from an article by an education researcher. Both concern policies that keep students from using their phones during the school day.
text:
PASSAGE A

Two years ago our school began asking students to lock their phones in a fabric pouch when they arrive in the morning. We did it because teachers asked, not because of any study. The pouch stays with the student, but it cannot be opened without a magnet mounted by the front door, so for six and a half hours the phone is present and useless. I expected a revolt, and so did most of my staff. What I got was about three weeks of grumbling, a handful of pouches cut open with scissors, and then something I had not expected at all: noise.

The first thing teachers noticed was the cafeteria. For years lunch had been oddly quiet, a room of two hundred teenagers each looking down. Within a month it was loud again, loud in the old way, with card games and arguments and people laughing at things across the table rather than on a screen. Teachers reported fewer students asking to leave class for the bathroom, a request that had often been cover for checking messages. Our counselors saw fewer conflicts that had begun online during the school day and spilled into the hallway by afternoon. One teacher told me she had forgotten what her students looked like when they were bored, because for years they had never been bored; they had simply looked at their phones.

I am wary of claiming too much. Our test scores rose slightly the first year, but they had been rising before, and I cannot prove the pouches deserve the credit. Parents raised a serious concern about emergencies, and we answered it by making sure every classroom has a working telephone and by reminding families that in a real crisis a building full of students on their phones can make things harder, not easier. Not every student is won over, either. A senior told me in the spring that she resented being treated like a child in her last year before college, and I thought she had a point; seniors now keep their phones at lunch. Still, I have worked in schools for twenty-six years, and I know what a room of students paying attention to one another feels like. I had nearly forgotten.

PASSAGE B

Few school policies have spread as quickly in recent years as the ban on phones, and few have been adopted on so little evidence. The case for bans rests mainly on accounts like the principal’s, and I do not doubt those accounts. Principals and teachers are close observers of their own buildings. When they say a cafeteria is louder and a hallway calmer, they are very likely right. My concern is with what happens when their observations are treated as proof of something else.

The difficulty is that a calmer building is not the same thing as better learning, and the studies that have tried to measure learning have produced mixed results. Some comparisons of schools before and after a ban have found modest gains in test scores, especially among students who had been struggling. Others have found little or no change. Many of these studies are small, and schools that adopt bans often change other things at the same time, which makes it hard to know what caused what. A policy that is easy to announce and visible to parents can spread for reasons that have little to do with whether it works. The honest summary is that we do not yet know whether bans improve achievement, and if they do, by how much.

I am also uneasy about what a ban teaches. A student who spends the school day with a locked phone learns that phones are dangerous, but she does not learn how to manage one, and she will leave school at three o’clock with the same device and none of the practice. Learning to put a phone down is a skill, and skills need practice. Adults have not solved this problem either; most of us check our phones far more often than we would like. A school that simply removes the temptation may be doing students a kindness for seven hours and a disservice for the rest of their lives. I would rather see bans treated as experiments, measured carefully, and paired with teaching that might last longer than the pouch.

title: Two Views on Moving Species Ahead of Climate Change
blurb: Passage A is adapted from an essay by a forest ecologist. Passage B is adapted from an article by a conservation biologist. Both concern assisted migration, the deliberate moving of species to places where the climate is expected to suit them.
text:
PASSAGE A

Trees migrate, but slowly. When the glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, many North American tree species moved northward behind them at rates that, by some reconstructions, averaged a few hundred meters a year, spreading one generation of seeds at a time. Species whose heavy seeds fall close to the parent tree moved more slowly still. That pace served them well when the climate was changing over millennia. It is unlikely to serve them now. In many regions the band of climate suitable for a given species is shifting faster than the species can follow, and a tree that cannot keep up will eventually find itself rooted in a place that no longer suits it.

Assisted migration proposes a simple answer: if a species cannot reach its future range on its own, we can carry it there. Foresters in some places already practice a cautious version of this, planting seedlings from warmer, more southern sources a little north of where they would otherwise be planted, so that the forests growing now will suit the climate expected when they mature. A bolder version moves a species well beyond its current range. A group of volunteers, for instance, has planted seedlings of the Florida torreya, a rare conifer whose small native population has been declining for decades, in forests several hundred miles to the north.

The torreya is a useful example because it is so small a gamble. It is a slow-growing tree that is not known to have spread aggressively anywhere, its seedlings are easy to monitor, and if the experiment went badly they could be removed. Not every candidate will be so easy. But the species that most need help are, almost by definition, the rare and struggling ones, and rare, struggling species are not usually the ones that overrun a forest.

I understand the objection that moving species is dangerous, and I do not dismiss it. But the danger has to be weighed against the alternative, which is not a safe status quo. It is the loss of species that are already stranded. Doing nothing is also a choice with consequences, and those consequences are becoming easier to see every year. Every year of delay narrows the choices that remain.

PASSAGE B

The history of moving species on purpose is, on the whole, a history of disasters. In 1935, cane toads were released in northeastern Australia to control beetles in the sugarcane fields. They did little to the beetles and spread across much of the continent, poisoning native predators that tried to eat them. Mongooses brought to several islands to control rats ate native birds and reptiles instead. Each of these introductions was made by people who were confident they understood the species they were moving. Several of the animals introduced in this way are now among the costliest pests in the places they were taken to.

Advocates of assisted migration reply that moving a species a few hundred miles within its own continent is different from shipping toads across an ocean, and they are partly right. The risks are smaller. They are not zero. A tree moved north arrives with its own insects and fungi, and meets new ones, and nobody can predict with confidence how those encounters will go. Nor is it clear that a moved species will do what its planters hope. It may fail quietly, or it may succeed too well.

There is also the question of who decides. The torreya plantings were carried out by private volunteers rather than by any agency charged with weighing the risks, and some critics objected less to the tree than to the precedent. If anyone who believes a species is in danger may move it wherever seems best, the result could be thousands of small experiments with no one keeping track of them.

I would not rule assisted migration out entirely. For a species with a tiny population and nowhere left to go, the calculation may change. But for most species, the better investment is to protect and connect the habitats they already have, so that they can move on their own along corridors of land, at whatever speed they can manage. That approach is slower and less dramatic. Its mistakes, however, are far easier to undo, and it helps species we have not yet thought to worry about.
